    in the section on extension traits). In all other cases where you want to implement functionality for a type, use an inherent implementation . Don’t use traits merely to organize code. Extension traits An extension trait is a trait that adds methods to a type from a different crate. What differentiates an extension trait from other traits is that its sole
    purpose is to add methods to the type; it is not intended for use in generics
    ( T: Trait , impl Trait ) or dynamic dispatch ( dyn Trait ). To indicate this,
    the name of an extension trait should carry the suffix ~Ext (for example, ForeignTypeExt ). In general, the team that owns the original type should also own the extension
    trait. Exceptions: Extension methods that are expected to become well known and provide
    significant value, for example, in foundational libraries / frameworks. Note: This rule is specifically about extension traits. It is relatively common
    to define a trait as an input trait (e.g., DateLike ) and implement it on a
    bunch of foreign types. Examples extern crate foreign_crate ; use foreign_crate :: ForeignType ; trait ForeignTypeExt { fn additional_method ( & self ); } impl ForeignTypeExt for ForeignType { fn additional_method ( & self ) { ... } } It is also possible to define an extension trait for every type that implements
    some foreign trait. Effectively, this is equivalent to adding default methods to
    the foreign trait: extern crate foreign_crate ; use foreign_crate :: ForeignTrait ; trait ForeignTraitExt { fn additional_method ( & self ); } impl < T : ForeignTrait > ForeignTraitExt for T { fn additional_method ( & self ) { ... } } Rationale When the same team owns the extension trait and the type being extended, this
    helps avoid method name conflicts between the base type and the extension trait
    or between two extension traits. Specific guidance for important traits Types with public fields : Consider implementing traits implemented by
    all subfields. Error types : Implement the Copy trait whenever possible. Copy types
    are simpler to manage and propagate because they can be passed by value
    without moving ownership. An example of a case where this is not possible is
    if the error must contain non- Copy fields like a String . Copy : Implement whenever it is reasonably clear that the type will
    continue to be Copy in the future. Clone : Most types should implement Clone unless they represent some
    external resource. Default : Implement if the type implements new() or otherwise has a
    default state. For context, see Clippy lint new_without_default . PartialEq / Eq : If you want users to use the == operator,
    prefer implementing PartialEq over Eq . When you do implement Eq , be
    aware of the additionally required reflexivity (details:
    https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cmp/trait.Eq.html). PartialOrd / Ord : If you want users to use the < or > operators, prefer implementing PartialOrd over Ord . When you do
    implement Ord , be aware that it requires total ordering (details:
    https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cmp/trait.Ord.html). Map keys If you think it is likely that a type will be used as a map key or
    otherwise cached, implement Hash and Eq . If, in addition, the type has a clear total ordering, implement Ord (and any traits it needs). Pair important From impls with explicit constructor methods If a type has an important From impl that is expected to be one of the primary
    ways of constructing it, add an inherent ::new() , ::new_from_foo() ¸ or ::from_foo() method. Options structs should implement Default Structs with all-public fields that are primarily used as a “bag of options” for
    a function should implement Default . Rationale This enables convenient use of struct update syntax ( Struct { a: 0,
    ..Default::default()} ). Concurrency Handling poison Never reach inside a poisoned mutex to get at its insides, no matter how
    tempting the use case may seem. Don’t use async / .await [chrome] Don’t use async / .await in Chromium. </section> Don’t start new threads through the Rust standard library [chrome] In Chromium, prefer to use sequences instead of threads. Use fuchsia_sync::Mutex [Fuchsia] Use Fuchsia’s mutex type, rather than one from std::sync or parking_lot . Macros When considering how to express an API, prefer in order: Regular Rust functions, types, traits, objects, and modules. (Avoid macros,
    code generation, and metaprogramming where possible). macro_rules! -style macros. Other code generation strategies (e.g. genrule ) proc_macro macros. When you decide to use a macro or code generation, please weigh the benefits
    against the costs: IDEs, Code Search and other developer tools will work less well on code that
    uses macros. Macros can create dialects of the language that make it harder for engineers
    to work across the codebase. Large scale changes are more difficult and expensive to apply. Rationale Prefer non-macro facilities: Macros can create dialects of the language that
    make it harder for engineers to work across the codebase. When a reader sees a
    usage of a macro, they can make fewer assumptions about that code than if it
    didn’t use a macro. Macros are harder to write correctly than regular Rust code. Use macro_rules! for simple code generation: Since Rust macros operate on
    the AST, they can be less fragile than textual code generation. Naming Naming methods Follow the Rust standard library style for naming methods. See also the guidance
    on naming conventions in the Comprehensive Rust course. Specific considerations: Use prefixes such as as_...() , to_...() , or into_...() with the
    appropriate self convention. See also this section of the Rust API Guidelines and the Clippy lint wrong_self_convention . Naming lifetimes Lifetimes should have descriptive names, especially type lifetimes. Exceptions: Type lifetimes that are extremely generic abstractions like Cow . It is fine to use anonymous lifetimes ( '_ ) where they work. Single-character lifetimes are okay when they are simply expressing the
    relationship between a method’s input and output, or needed for a local
    higher-ranked lifetime bounds ( for<'a> ). Up to two such local lifetimes
    are fine, if more are needed, we strongly advise you to use descriptive
    names. Naming generic parameters Use a short name for your generic parameters (either single or multi character),
    related to the kind of thing they represent. Single-letter generics are okay,
    but the letter chosen should be somewhat indicative of the object type, ideally
    taken from the most important trait bound. T or U are fine when the generics are in a relatively unbound context; i.e.
    it is an API intended for use with most types, like Vec<T> . Naming extension traits When naming an extension trait , give the name an ~Ext suffix (for example, ForeignTypeExt ). Naming initialization functions Follow these guidelines when naming initialization functions: Constructors: Use new() , or new_with_foo() if there is more than one. If
    the constructor returns a Result , use try_new() . Value-to-value conversions: Use from_foo() with an associated From impl.
    See here for details on when an operation can be considered to be a value-to-value
    conversion. Avoid abbreviations Don’t use abbreviations (especially acronyms and initialisms) that someone
    outside your project is unlikely to know. Don’t abbreviate by deleting letters
    within a word. See also the Google C++ Style Guide . Exceptions: Common abbreviations found in Wikipedia. Abbreviations that are unlikely to be confusing to people outside of your
    project, for example IpAddr . You and your reviewer should make this
    determination. In general, the preference should still be not to abbreviate. When and how to write documentation Add documentation comments to public APIs, potentially using the missing_doc lint to help with this. Best practices for documentation comments: Consider including examples: It is not necessary for every function to have
    examples, but enough functionality should be covered in examples somewhere to give an idea of how the crate works. Always document panic cases for functions which may panic due to malformed
    input. Clearly document invariants for unsafe functions and traits. Use capitalization and punctuation. Don’t explain the basics of the programming language. For example, don’t do
    the following: struct MockFileSystem { ... } /// A mock implementation of the FileSystem trait, intended to be used in unit tests. impl FileSystem for MockFileSystem Exceptions: Comments should say something that the code does not already say. If there’s
    nothing insightful to say, it is better to omit the comment than to repeat
    the function name in a trivial way. For example, don’t do the following
    (it’s fine to allow the lint in that case): /// Removes an element. pub fn remove_element () -> Element {} It is generally okay to omit documentation on individual enum variants,
    especially if their name is self-explanatory. How to format documentation comments Follow these guidelines when writing documentation comments: Use /// comments to document items following the comment, such as
    functions, structs, enums, traits, and type aliases. Use //! comments to document the module or the library itself. These
    comments should be placed at the top of the file. Follow the rules laid out in the official Rust style guide on doc comments . Use Markdown syntax. Use ordinary comment syntax ( // ) for non-documentation comments, such as
    implementation comments, TODOs that are not interesting for users, commented
    out source code, etc. Prefer to document things in a straightforward manner, using /// and //! comments, rather than generating documentation from macros. This makes the
    documentation directly readable when viewing or modifying the source code. It is acceptable, and even encouraged, to mix doc comments ( /// and //! ) and
    ordinary comments ( // ). If you have one thing you wish to document publicly,
    and another thing you want to note as an implementation comment, then use both!
    For example: /// Finds the first `FooItem` with the given `name`, or `None` if not present. // TODO: crbug.com/12345 - `name` should be &str, not String. pub fn get_named ( items : & [ FooItem ], name : String ) -> Option <& FooItem > { ... } Rationale Many, though not all, languages have a different commenting convention (such as
    extra * characters) for doc comments as opposed to implementation comments.
    Rust and Python are notable for not just having different commenting
    conventions, but an actual different syntax entirely. This has concrete benefits
    to the Rust ecosystem: Doc comments can be consumed by tooling, including documentation generators
    like rustdoc , IDE features, and Kythe. Doc comments have a standard structure and formatting rules (Markdown),
    allowing for rich text in those contexts. Errors in applying doc comment syntax (e.g., applying it to an expression
    instead of a documentable item) are linted against, catching documentation
    errors early. If there are no lint errors, the doc comments are guaranteed
    to be visible to documentation tooling, removing a degree of flakiness and
    unpredictability from the documentation process. Doc comments are a part of the AST, and so can be produced and consumed by
    macros, including both macro_rules! macros and procedural macros. Other Rust features Unsafe code Don’t write unsafe code unless there is no way to implement the same
    functionality with safe code. If you do have to write unsafe code: Encapsulate unsafe code in a safe abstraction and isolate it from business
    logic as much as possible. Ideally, unsafe code should be in a separate
    crate with few dependencies beyond the standard library. Add a safety comment starting with SAFETY: that explains why the code is
    correct. Add a technical justification for unsafe code. Depending on context, this
    can be a justification for an individual unsafe block or a more general
    justification that covers an entire file or build target. The justification
    should answer these questions: Why is this code not written in an equivalent safe way? If the reason is performance, are there benchmarks? No unstable features Don’t use unstable features. Exceptions: Android Embedded programming may require the
    use of certain unstable features. While review will be required to enable
    them (to help search for alternatives), features absolutely required to
    build an artifact correctly will generally be approved. Chrome Style arbiters may blanket-approve a
    small list of features for the entire codebase. Typically, only features
    that have a clear path to stabilization will be approved. Fuchsia See guidance here . Getters and setters Writing and naming getters and setters should follow these guidelines: foo() for a getter that returns a T by value. foo_mut() for a getter that returns a &mut T . take_foo() for a getter that “clears” the value (by setting it to None or some other default state) and returns the old value. set_foo() for a setter that takes a T by value. with_foo() / with_mut_foo() for an accessor that operates via a closure
    (see details below ). Such an accessor is invoked as object.with_foo(|foo| frob(foo)) . replace_foo() for a setter that returns the old value. Examples impl Stuff { fn foo ( & self ) -> & Foo { ... } fn foo_mut ( & mut self ) -> & mut Foo { ... } /// Sets "baz" property to `None` and returns the old value. fn take_baz ( & mut self ) -> Option < Baz > { ... } fn set_foo ( & mut self , foo : Foo ) { ... } /// Calls `f` with a borrow of the "bar" property. /// Returns the return value of `f`. fn with_bar < R > ( & self , f : impl FnOnce ( & Bar ) -> R ) -> R { ... } /// Calls `f` with a mutable borrow of the "bar" property. /// Returns the return value of `f`. fn with_mut_bar < R > ( & self , f : impl FnOnce ( & mut i32 ) -> R ) -> R { ... } /// Sets "foo" property to `foo` and returns the old value. fn replace_foo ( & mut self , foo : Foo ) -> Foo { ... } } More on accessors that accept closures Accessors that accept a closure ( .with_foo() ) are typically invoked as object.with_foo(|foo| do_something_with(foo)) . They can be a good choice in
    the following situations: When the property is contained in an interior mutability wrapper (e.g. Mutex or RefCell ). These mechanisms need to constrain access to the
    property to a scope, and the closure provides this scope. This is usually
    preferable to directly returning the RAII object that implements the scope
    (e.g. MutexGuard<T> ) because the latter would leak an implementation
    detail. When follow-up work or validation is needed after a property is changed and
    a set_foo() accessor cannot be used (for example because the property’s
    type is expensive to clone or cannot be cloned at all). A with_foo() accessor will often allow the closure to return a value and
    forward it by returning it from with_foo() . If you need to provide two closure-accepting accessors, one for read-only access
    and one for mutable access, it is common to name them with_foo() and with_mut_foo() . Otherwise, with_foo() is often also used for mutating
    accessors. Implement expected API sets together If you implement len() , also implement is_empty() . For context, see Clippy
    lint len_without_is_empty . Do not access items marked #[doc(hidden)] that you don’t own Treat items marked #[doc(hidden)] as private. Don’t access them unless you own
    the code. Use const functions responsibly Mark a public function as const only if you expect it to remain const in the
    future (or can commit to helping clients migrate when it changes). Rationale It’s a breaking change to turn a const function into a regular function. Avoid overloading for non-mathematical purposes Use operator overloads for their original mathematical/logical purpose, not just
    to make the code more concise (as “syntax sugar”). Apply #[non_exhaustive] to publicly-exposed enums If an enum is part of a public API used by other teams, mark it #[non_exhaustive] . Exceptions: The enum will never change. For example: Enums describing an existing ontology (e.g., enum Color { Red, Green,
    Blue } ). Enums with two states that could be Booleans (e.g., enum Visibility {
    Visible, Hidden } ) The enum may change in the future, but you are committed to fixing
    resulting breakages via an LSC. For context, see Clippy lint exhaustive_enums . Rationale Marking an enum #[non_exhaustive] forces users to include a wildcard arm ( _
    => ... ) in match statements. This ensures code continues to compile when new
    variants are added to the enum later. This rule is primarily important for enums used across team boundaries, because
    the scope of the breakage could be significant. Enums used only a small number
    of times can’t create a large breakage and thus may ignore this rule. Apply #[non_exhaustive] to public structs with public fields Structs with public fields that are part of a public API used by other teams
    should be marked #[non_exhaustive] . Exceptions: The struct fields are unlikely to change, e.g., because they describe an
    existing ontology (e.g., a Rectangle type) or the reviewer can otherwise be
    confident that they will not change. The struct fields may change in the future, but you are committed to
    fixing resulting breakages via an LSC. You want to enable your users to use functional record update (FRU) struct
    initialization syntax ( Person { name: "foo", ..Default::default() } ). Rationale Adding a new field (even a private one) to a struct with all public fields is a
    breaking change, because callers can no longer name all fields in a struct
    literal. A #[non_exhaustive] struct can’t be constructed with the struct literal
    syntax, except for the code in the same crate. This allows new private fields to
    be added without breaking users. This rule is primarily important for structs used across team boundaries,
    because the scope of the breakage could be significant. Structs used only a
    small number of times can’t create a large breakage and thus may ignore this
    rule. #[must_use] on functions Use #[must_use] on functions in these cases: The caller cannot use the function correctly if they ignore the return
    value. This includes pure functions (functions without side effects), such
    as HashMap::get() . Any function whose return value represents an error or otherwise critical
    information about the function’s behavior. If the return type is already
    annotated #[must_use] (which is true of Result , for example), the
    function does not need to be annotated #[must_use] . #[must_use] on types Use #[must_use] on types intended to be returned by functions that would
    otherwise be annotated #[must_use] according to the rules above . Examples: The type is an error type (similar to Result or StatusOr ). The type represents a lazily evaluated computation. In other words, the
    function call doesn’t do anything by itself, and the return value needs to
    be accessed to cause some desired side effect. Do not run code before main() Do not cause code to run before main() , for example by using techniques such
    as the ctor crate . Implementation concerns Don’t overuse type inference Add enough explicit types so that someone familiar with the codebase can figure
    out what the inferred types are. Prefer to add the types to variable declarations, rather than as turbofishes . If
    the compiler forces you to add a turbofish, it is generally fine to add a _ inference marker. Specific situations in which you should probably add types: When calling methods with a generic return type, such as .into() or .parse() . For the result of complex iterator chains. Prefer pattern matching over check-then-unwrap Avoid potentially panicking operations when the input data guarantees they
    cannot panic. For example, instead of using Option::unwrap on a value known to
    be valid, use pattern matching to prove correctness to the compiler. // Good: The match arm proves to the compiler that `x` is `Some`. // A panic is obviously not possible. if let Some ( value ) = option { use_value ( value ); } // Bad: Correctness of `unwrap` relies on a runtime check that `option` is `Some`. if option .is_some () { use_value ( option .unwrap ()); } Prefer expect over unwrap If a panic is necessary because an invariant cannot be expressed in the type
    system, prefer expect over unwrap to document the reason. Don’t omit patterns on non_exhaustive enums when matching Prefer to list all enum variants in match statements over non_exhaustive enums. If you don’t care about specific variants, place them in the wildcard arm. If
    you only care about specific variants, use an if let or a let … else {} . Examples: #[non_exhaustive] pub enum Shape { Circle , Square , Triangle , } fn process_shape ( shape : Shape ) { match shape { Shape :: Circle => println! ( "It's a circle" ), Shape :: Square => println! ( "It's a square" ), // Triangle and any future variants don't require any actions. Shape :: Triangle | _ => {} } } fn process_shape ( shape : Shape ) { if let Shape :: Circle = shape { println! ( "It's a circle" ), } } fn process_shape ( shape : Shape ) { match shape { Shape :: Circle => println! ( "It's a circle" ), _ => {} } } Exceptions: You only care about specific variants and match is cleaner than if
    let . This is covered by the built-in lint non_exhaustive_omitted_patterns which you
    can enable on your code. Use context strings to clarify assertions While some assertions are self-explanatory, many benefit from additional context
    that clarifies why an assertion is expected to hold, or what caused it to be
    violated. Use the optional format string argument for assert! to convey this
    context. You should always consider adding context, but particularly in the following
    situations: If you’re thinking of adding a comment to the assertion. Use a format string
    instead: It has the benefit that it will appear in logs. If you expect failing assertions to be seen by users. In this case, a
    human-readable explanation is more helpful than a Rust expression. If logging a value helps in understanding why the assertion failed. To clarify whether a failing assertion means that The client misused an API (i.e., they should change their use of the
    API), or The implementation contains a bug (i.e., the client should file a bug
    report). Examples Explaining why an assertion should hold assert! ( values .is_sorted (), "`values` is populated from a `PriorityQueue`, so we expect it to be sorted" ); Logging a value to clarify why the assertion failed assert! ( refund > 0 , "Refund must be positive, got {refund:?}); Flagging misuse of an API impl Database { ... fn execute_query ( & self , query : & str ) { assert! ( self .stream .is_some (), "Call connect() before executing queries" ); } ... } Don’t use the context string merely to repeat the condition assert ( ! values .is_sorted (), "values should always be sorted" ); Don’t use iterator combinator chains when direct iteration is clearer Avoid using combinator chains in ways that hurt readability. Specifically: Avoid long and complex combinator chains. Don’t construct combinator chains in the header of a for loop. Instead,
    assign the combinator chain to a variable, then consume that variable in the for loop. Avoid Iterator::for_each unless you’re convinced you have a good reason. A for loop is usually easier to read. Combinators are preferable for shorter chains and for cases where the
    combinator itself provides a lot of logic that would otherwise have to be
    written out in the corresponding for loop. Examples Complex combinator chains Here’s an example of a combinator chain that is hard to read because it involves
    conditionals and mutates external state: let mut error_count = 0 ; let _processed_items : Vec < _ > = items .into_iter () .map ( transformation_that_may_fail ) .map (| result | { if result .is_err () { error_count += 1 ; } result }) .filter_map ( Result :: ok ) .collect (); The corresponding for loop is easier to read: let mut error_count = 0 ; let mut processed_items = Vec :: with_capacity ( items .len ()); for item in items { match transformation_that_may_fail ( item ) { Ok ( val ) => processed_items .push ( val ), Err ( _ ) => error_count += 1 , } } Combinator chains in for loops Avoid constructing a combinator chain in the header of a for loop: for bug in bug_descriptions .iter () .filter_map (| description | parse_bug_description ( description ) .ok ()) .filter (| bug | bug .priority <= Priority :: P1 ) { assign_bug ( bug ); } Instead, assign the combinator chain to a variable. This reduces clutter, and
    the variable name documents what the combinator chain does: let urgent_bugs = bug_descriptions .iter () .filter_map (| description | parse_bug_description ( description ) .ok ()) .filter (| bug | bug .priority <= Priority :: P1 ); for bug in urgent_bugs { assign_bug ( bug ); } When to prefer a combinator chain Here’s an example where a combinator chain is preferable: let threshold_exceeded = values .iter () .any (| & v | v > threshold ); The corresponding for loop is harder to read and reinvents the logic contained
    in any() : let mut threshold_exceeded = false ; for v in values { if v > threshold { threshold_exceeded = true ; break ; } } Don’t call panic::catch_unwind Use of panic::catch_unwind is prohibited in first-party Rust code. Exceptions: It is acceptable as a defense in depth mechanism as long as it is never relied upon for any properties. A codebase that is already attempting to
    avoid panics may choose to wrap critical entry points with a catch_unwind recovery mechanism just in case a panic slips through. Code authors must
    convince the reviewer that the codebase is doing most of what it can to
    avoid panics. This exception only applies to code that has the possibility
    of being run with panic=unwind (so this does not apply to Chrome , Android , Fuchsia ). Rationale Rust code may be used in many environments, and panic::catch_unwind will only
    function correctly in environments with panic=unwind . While the final panic
    disposition of prod binaries has not yet been determined, Chrome, Android, and
    Fuchsia all require panic=abort . Prefer format! / write! for concatenation and substitution Prefer format!() and write!() to other alternatives in the following
    situations: To concatenate more than two strings. For example, use format!("{a}{b}{c}") instead of a + b + c . To perform substitutions on a literal string (instead of using str::replace ). Rationale format! / write! require fewer allocations than concatenating strings
    using + . Prefer standard format strings to inventing your own templating syntax. Use the right per-codebase test framework Most codebases use their own specific test framework rather than #[test] . Chrome Use rust_gtest_interop .
    This makes it possible to integrate Rust tests into C++ test binaries. Fuchsia Use #[fuchsia::test] . See here for more details. This site is open source. Improve this page . anchors.add();

    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
        Configures and builds the native worker against a pinned Azahar tree.
    
    .DESCRIPTION
        One build directory per branch. The integration and the experimental
        branch must never share a configured CMake cache.
    
        Example:
          scripts\build-azahar.ps1 -Branch integration
          scripts\build-azahar.ps1 -Branch experimental
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param(
        [ValidateSet('integration', 'experimental')]
        [string]$Branch = 'integration',
    
        [ValidateSet('Debug', 'Release')]
        [string]$Profile = 'Release',
    
        [string]$AzaharRoot,
        [string]$BuildDirectory
    )
    
    $ErrorActionPreference = 'Continue'
    if (Get-Variable -Name PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue) {
        $PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference = $false
    }
    $root = Split-Path -Parent $PSScriptRoot
    Import-Module (Join-Path $PSScriptRoot 'Pins.psm1') -Force
    
    $pins = Read-Pins -Path (Join-Path $root 'config\pins.toml')
    
    if (-not $AzaharRoot) {
        $AzaharRoot = Join-Path $root $pins['azahar']['vendor_path']
    }
    
    if (-not $BuildDirectory) {
        $BuildDirectory = Join-Path $root ("build\azahar-" + $Branch)
    }
    
    if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $AzaharRoot)) {
        Write-Error "no Azahar tree at $AzaharRoot. Run scripts\bootstrap.ps1 first."
    }
    
    Write-Host "==> Configuring the $Branch worker" -ForegroundColor Cyan
    Write-Host "    azahar tree : $AzaharRoot"
    Write-Host "    build dir   : $BuildDirectory"
    
    & cmake -S (Join-Path $root 'workers\azahar') -B $BuildDirectory `
        -DLOTUS_AZAHAR_ROOT=$AzaharRoot `
        "-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=$Profile"
    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) {
        Write-Error 'CMake configuration failed'
    }
    
    Write-Host '==> Building' -ForegroundColor Cyan
    & cmake --build $BuildDirectory --config $Profile
    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) {
        Write-Error 'the build failed'
    }
    
    Write-Host ''
    Write-Host "worker built in $BuildDirectory" -ForegroundColor Green

    //! Request/reply/event envelope shared by every IPC channel.
    
    use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
    
    use crate::error::{ProtocolError, Result};
    
    /// Maximum payload accepted in a single envelope.
    ///
    /// Every request must define a maximum. This is the hard ceiling enforced
    /// before any allocation happens.
    pub const MAX_PAYLOAD_LEN: u32 = 64 * 1024 * 1024;
    
    /// Kind of message carried by an envelope.
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[repr(u8)]
    pub enum EnvelopeKind {
        /// A request from a client to a worker.
        Request = 1,
        /// A reply to a previously issued request.
        Reply = 2,
        /// An unsolicited event from a worker.
        Event = 3,
    }
    
    impl EnvelopeKind {
        /// Convert a wire byte into an envelope kind.
        pub fn from_wire(value: u8) -> Result<Self> {
            match value {
                1 => Ok(Self::Request),
                2 => Ok(Self::Reply),
                3 => Ok(Self::Event),
                other => Err(ProtocolError::Malformed(format!(
                    "unknown envelope kind {other}"
                ))),
            }
        }
    }
    
    /// Fixed-size session identifier.
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, PartialOrd, Ord)]
    pub struct SessionUuid(pub [u8; 16]);
    
    impl SessionUuid {
        /// Generate a random session identifier.
        pub fn generate() -> Self {
            // A random value is good enough for a per-run local identifier; it is
            // never used as a security token.
            let mut bytes = [0u8; 16];
            let nanos = std::time::SystemTime::now()
                .duration_since(std::time::UNIX_EPOCH)
                .map(|d| d.as_nanos())
                .unwrap_or_default();
            let pid = std::process::id() as u128;
            let mut state = nanos ^ (pid << 64) ^ 0x9E37_79B9_7F4A_7C15;
            for byte in bytes.iter_mut() {
                // xorshift64*
                state ^= state >> 12;
                state ^= state << 25;
                state ^= state >> 27;
                let value = state.wrapping_mul(0x2545_F491_4F6C_DD1D);
                *byte = (value >> 32) as u8;
            }
            Self(bytes)
        }
    
        /// Raw bytes of the identifier.
        pub fn as_bytes(&self) -> &[u8; 16] {
            &self.0
        }
    }
    
    impl std::fmt::Display for SessionUuid {
        fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
            for byte in self.0.iter() {
                write!(f, "{byte:02x}")?;
            }
            Ok(())
        }
    }
    
    /// Header of every IPC message.
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
    pub struct EnvelopeHeader {
        /// Protocol major version of the sender.
        pub version_major: u16,
        /// Protocol minor version of the sender.
        pub version_minor: u16,
        /// Identifier of the request this message belongs to.
        pub request_id: u64,
        /// Session the message belongs to.
        pub session_uuid: SessionUuid,
        /// State epoch the message was produced in.
        pub session_epoch: u64,
        /// Message kind.
        pub kind: EnvelopeKind,
        /// Length of the payload that follows.
        pub payload_len: u32,
    }
    
    impl EnvelopeHeader {
        /// Build a header for a message of `payload_len` bytes.
        pub fn new(
            request_id: u64,
            session_uuid: SessionUuid,
            session_epoch: u64,
            kind: EnvelopeKind,
            payload_len: u32,
        ) -> Self {
            Self {
                version_major: crate::PROTOCOL_VERSION_MAJOR,
                version_minor: crate::PROTOCOL_VERSION_MINOR,
                request_id,
                session_uuid,
                session_epoch,
                kind,
                payload_len,
            }
        }
    
        /// Reject payloads that exceed the hard ceiling before allocating.
        pub fn check_payload_len(&self) -> Result<()> {
            if self.payload_len > MAX_PAYLOAD_LEN {
                return Err(ProtocolError::PayloadTooLarge {
                    len: self.payload_len,
                    max: MAX_PAYLOAD_LEN,
                });
            }
            Ok(())
        }
    }
    
    #[cfg(test)]
    mod tests {
        use super::*;
    
        #[test]
        fn generated_uuids_differ() {
            let a = SessionUuid::generate();
            let b = SessionUuid::generate();
            assert_ne!(a, b);
            assert_eq!(a.to_string().len(), 32);
        }
    
        #[test]
        fn payload_limit_is_enforced() {
            let header = EnvelopeHeader::new(
                1,
                SessionUuid::generate(),
                0,
                EnvelopeKind::Request,
                MAX_PAYLOAD_LEN + 1,
            );
            assert!(matches!(
                header.check_payload_len(),
                Err(ProtocolError::PayloadTooLarge { .. })
            ));
        }
    
        #[test]
        fn envelope_kind_round_trips() {
            for kind in [
                EnvelopeKind::Request,
                EnvelopeKind::Reply,
                EnvelopeKind::Event,
            ] {
                assert_eq!(EnvelopeKind::from_wire(kind as u8).unwrap(), kind);
            }
            assert!(EnvelopeKind::from_wire(9).is_err());
        }
    }
    //! Protocol level errors.
    
    use thiserror::Error;
    
    /// Result alias for protocol operations.
    pub type Result<T> = std::result::Result<T, ProtocolError>;
    
    /// Errors raised by the protocol layer.
    #[derive(Debug, Error, PartialEq, Eq)]
    pub enum ProtocolError {
        /// The peer speaks an incompatible protocol version.
        #[error("incompatible protocol version: peer {peer_major}.{peer_minor}, local {local_major}.{local_minor}")]
        IncompatibleVersion {
            /// Peer major version.
            peer_major: u16,
            /// Peer minor version.
            peer_minor: u16,
            /// Local major version.
            local_major: u16,
            /// Local minor version.
            local_minor: u16,
        },
        /// The payload exceeds the enforced maximum.
        #[error("payload too large: {len} bytes, maximum is {max}")]
        PayloadTooLarge {
            /// Observed payload length.
            len: u32,
            /// Enforced maximum.
            max: u32,
        },
        /// The message could not be decoded.
        #[error("malformed message: {0}")]
        Malformed(String),
        /// The request is not known to this build.
        #[error("unknown request: {0}")]
        UnknownRequest(String),
        /// The worker is not running or not reachable.
        #[error("worker unavailable: {0}")]
        WorkerUnavailable(String),
        /// The worker did not answer in time.
        #[error("worker timed out after {0} ms")]
        Timeout(u64),
        /// A read or write was rejected by the worker.
        #[error("operation rejected: {0}")]
        Rejected(String),
    }
    
    #[cfg(test)]
    mod tests {
        use super::*;
    
        #[test]
        fn errors_display_without_panicking() {
            let error = ProtocolError::IncompatibleVersion {
                peer_major: 2,
                peer_minor: 0,
                local_major: 1,
                local_minor: 0,
            };
            assert!(error.to_string().contains("2.0"));
        }
    }
    //! Native worker process handling.
    //!
    //! The worker is a separate OS process running a modified Azahar core. This
    //! module owns starting it, handing it its private storage and stopping it
    //! without leaving orphans behind.
    
    use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
    use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};
    use std::process::{Child, Command, Stdio};
    use thiserror::Error;
    
    /// Azahar branch flavour a worker was built from.
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]
    pub enum WorkerFlavor {
        /// `integration` branch: upstream minimal worker hooks.
        Integration,
        /// `experimental` branch: tracing, debugger and accuracy work.
        Experimental,
    }
    
    impl WorkerFlavor {
        /// Branch name on the Azahar fork.
        pub fn branch(&self) -> &'static str {
            match self {
                WorkerFlavor::Integration => "integration",
                WorkerFlavor::Experimental => "experimental",
            }
        }
    }
    
    /// Errors raised while launching or supervising a worker.
    #[derive(Debug, Error)]
    pub enum WorkerLaunchError {
        /// The worker executable was not found.
        #[error("worker executable not found: {0}")]
        NotFound(PathBuf),
        /// The worker could not be started.
        #[error("failed to launch worker: {0}")]
        Launch(#[source] std::io::Error),
    }
    
    /// How a worker process should be started.
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
    pub struct WorkerSpec {
        /// Path of the worker executable.
        pub executable: PathBuf,
        /// Private storage root handed to the worker.
        pub storage_root: PathBuf,
        /// Additional command line arguments.
        pub args: Vec<String>,
        /// Environment variables added to the worker environment.
        pub env: Vec<(String, String)>,
    }
    
    impl WorkerSpec {
        /// A worker that runs against `storage_root`.
        pub fn new(executable: impl Into<PathBuf>, storage_root: impl Into<PathBuf>) -> Self {
            Self {
                executable: executable.into(),
                storage_root: storage_root.into(),
                args: Vec::new(),
                env: Vec::new(),
            }
        }
    
        /// Add a command line argument.
        pub fn arg(mut self, arg: impl Into<String>) -> Self {
            self.args.push(arg.into());
            self
        }
    
        /// Add an environment variable.
        pub fn env(mut self, key: impl Into<String>, value: impl Into<String>) -> Self {
            self.env.push((key.into(), value.into()));
            self
        }
    }
    
    /// A running worker process.
    #[derive(Debug)]
    pub struct WorkerProcess {
        child: Child,
        executable: PathBuf,
    }
    
    impl WorkerProcess {
        /// Start a worker.
        pub fn spawn(spec: &WorkerSpec) -> Result<Self, WorkerLaunchError> {
            if !spec.executable.is_file() {
                return Err(WorkerLaunchError::NotFound(spec.executable.clone()));
            }
    
            let mut command = Command::new(&spec.executable);
            command
                .args(&spec.args)
                .envs(spec.env.iter().cloned())
                .env("LOTUS_STORAGE_ROOT", &spec.storage_root)
                .stdin(Stdio::null())
                .stdout(Stdio::null())
                .stderr(Stdio::null());
    
            #[cfg(windows)]
            {
                use std::os::windows::process::CommandExt;
                // Do not let the worker pop a console window on Windows.
                command.creation_flags(0x0800_0000);
            }
    
            let child = command.spawn().map_err(WorkerLaunchError::Launch)?;
            Ok(Self {
                child,
                executable: spec.executable.clone(),
            })
        }
    
        /// Process id of the worker.
        pub fn pid(&self) -> u32 {
            self.child.id()
        }
    
        /// Path of the worker executable.
        pub fn executable(&self) -> &Path {
            &self.executable
        }
    
        /// Whether the worker is still running.
        pub fn is_running(&mut self) -> bool {
            matches!(self.child.try_wait(), Ok(None))
        }
    
        /// Ask the worker to stop and wait for it, escalating if it ignores the
        /// request.
        pub fn terminate(&mut self) {
            if self.is_running() {
                let _ = self.child.kill();
            }
            let _ = self.child.wait();
        }
    }
    
    impl Drop for WorkerProcess {
        fn drop(&mut self) {
            self.terminate();
        }
    }
    
    #[cfg(test)]
    mod tests {
        use super::*;
    
        #[test]
        fn missing_executable_is_reported() {
            let spec = WorkerSpec::new(
                std::env::temp_dir().join("lotus-no-such-worker"),
                std::env::temp_dir().join("lotus-no-such-storage"),
            );
            assert!(matches!(
                WorkerProcess::spawn(&spec),
                Err(WorkerLaunchError::NotFound(_))
            ));
        }
    
        #[test]
        fn flavor_maps_to_branch_names() {
            assert_eq!(WorkerFlavor::Integration.branch(), "integration");
            assert_eq!(WorkerFlavor::Experimental.branch(), "experimental");
        }
    }
    //! Per-session private storage layout.
    //!
    //! Every session owns a directory tree that no other session writes to.
    //! NAND, save data, logs and captures live under it. Snapshots are copied in,
    //! never shared by reference, so two sessions started from the same snapshot
    //! cannot corrupt each other.
    
    use crate::SessionId;
    use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};
    
    /// Directory names created inside a session root.
    pub const NAND_DIR: &str = "nand";
    /// Save data directory.
    pub const SAVES_DIR: &str = "saves";
    /// Log directory.
    pub const LOGS_DIR: &str = "logs";
    /// Capture and trace directory.
    pub const CAPTURES_DIR: &str = "captures";
    /// Read only reference snapshots.
    pub const SNAPSHOTS_DIR: &str = "snapshots";
    
    /// Private storage layout of a session.
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
    pub struct StorageLayout {
        root: PathBuf,
    }
    
    impl StorageLayout {
        /// Create the directory tree for `id` below `base`.
        pub fn create(base: impl AsRef<Path>, id: SessionId) -> std::io::Result<Self> {
            let root = base.as_ref().join(id.to_string());
            for dir in [NAND_DIR, SAVES_DIR, LOGS_DIR, CAPTURES_DIR, SNAPSHOTS_DIR] {
                std::fs::create_dir_all(root.join(dir))?;
            }
            Ok(Self { root })
        }
    
        /// Session root directory.
        pub fn root(&self) -> &Path {
            &self.root
        }
    
        /// NAND directory.
        pub fn nand(&self) -> PathBuf {
            self.root.join(NAND_DIR)
        }
    
        /// Save data directory.
        pub fn saves(&self) -> PathBuf {
            self.root.join(SAVES_DIR)
        }
    
        /// Log directory.
        pub fn logs(&self) -> PathBuf {
            self.root.join(LOGS_DIR)
        }
    
        /// Capture directory.
        pub fn captures(&self) -> PathBuf {
            self.root.join(CAPTURES_DIR)
        }
    
        /// Snapshot directory.
        pub fn snapshots(&self) -> PathBuf {
            self.root.join(SNAPSHOTS_DIR)
        }
    }
    
    #[cfg(test)]
    mod tests {
        use super::*;
    
        #[test]
        fn create_makes_all_directories() {
            let base = std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("lotus-storage-test-{}", std::process::id()));
            let _ = std::fs::remove_dir_all(&base);
            let layout = StorageLayout::create(&base, SessionId(7)).unwrap();
            assert!(layout.nand().is_dir());
            assert!(layout.saves().is_dir());
            assert!(layout.logs().is_dir());
            assert!(layout.captures().is_dir());
            assert!(layout.snapshots().is_dir());
            let _ = std::fs::remove_dir_all(&base);
        }
    
        #[test]
        fn layout_is_per_session() {
            let base =
                std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("lotus-storage-test-2-{}", std::process::id()));
            let _ = std::fs::remove_dir_all(&base);
            let a = StorageLayout::create(&base, SessionId(1)).unwrap();
            let b = StorageLayout::create(&base, SessionId(2)).unwrap();
            assert_ne!(a.root(), b.root());
            let _ = std::fs::remove_dir_all(&base);
        }
    }
    [package]
    name = "lotus-session"
    version.workspace = true
    edition.workspace = true
    rust-version.workspace = true
    license.workspace = true
    authors.workspace = true
    repository.workspace = true
    description = "Worker process lifecycle, isolation and session state for the Rust application."
    
    [dependencies]
    lotus-protocol = { workspace = true }
    serde = { workspace = true }
    serde_json = { workspace = true }
    thiserror = { workspace = true }
    tracing = { workspace = true }
    //! `ctr-cli`: headless access to the Lotus tooling.
    //!
    //! The CLI shares the same typed operations as the desktop application and
    //! the MCP server. It never opens a window and never requires a GUI session.
    
    use anyhow::{bail, Context, Result};
    use lotus_protocol::protocol_id;
    use lotus_runner::Scenario;
    use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
    use std::path::PathBuf;
    
    /// Pinned revisions, mirrored from `config/pins.toml`.
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    struct Pins {
        azahar: AzaharPins,
        gpui: GpuiPins,
        rust: RustPins,
    }
    
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    struct AzaharPins {
        repository: String,
        fork: String,
        upstream_commit: String,
        integration_branch: String,
        integration_commit: String,
        experimental_branch: String,
        experimental_commit: String,
        vendor_path: String,
    }
    
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    struct GpuiPins {
        repository: String,
        rev: String,
        crate_version: String,
    }
    
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    struct RustPins {
        channel: String,
        host: String,
    }
    
    /// Usage text.
    const USAGE: &str = "\
    ctr-cli: Lotus command line interface
    
    Usage:
      ctr-cli version              Print the Lotus version and worker protocol version
      ctr-cli pins                 Print the pinned Azahar and GPUI revisions
      ctr-cli scenario validate <path>
                                    Validate a scenario file against the execution limits
    ";
    
    fn main() -> Result<()> {
        let args: Vec<String> = std::env::args().skip(1).collect();
        let command = args.first().map(String::as_str).unwrap_or("help");
    
        match command {
            "version" => {
                println!("lotus {}", env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"));
                println!("worker protocol {}", protocol_id());
            }
            "pins" => {
                let pins = load_pins()?;
                println!("{}", toml::to_string_pretty(&pins)?);
            }
            "scenario" => {
                let sub = args.get(1).map(String::as_str).unwrap_or("help");
                match sub {
                    "validate" => {
                        let path = args
                            .get(2)
                            .context("usage: ctr-cli scenario validate <path>")?;
                        let scenario = Scenario::load(path)
                            .with_context(|| format!("cannot load scenario {path}"))?;
                        scenario
                            .validate()
                            .with_context(|| format!("scenario {path} is invalid"))?;
                        println!("scenario {} is valid", scenario.name);
                    }
                    _ => {
                        println!("{USAGE}");
                        bail!("unknown scenario subcommand: {sub}");
                    }
                }
            }
            "help" | "--help" | "-h" => println!("{USAGE}"),
            other => {
                println!("{USAGE}");
                bail!("unknown command: {other}");
            }
        }
    
        Ok(())
    }
    
    /// Load the pinned revision manifest.
    fn load_pins() -> Result<Pins> {
        let path = pins_path();
        let text = std::fs::read_to_string(&path)
            .with_context(|| format!("cannot read {}", path.display()))?;
        toml::from_str(&text).with_context(|| format!("cannot parse {}", path.display()))
    }
    
    /// Location of the pinned revision manifest.
    fn pins_path() -> PathBuf {
        // The manifest lives in the repository root. Walk up from the crate
        // directory so the CLI works from a source checkout and from a build
        // directory inside the repository.
        let manifest = PathBuf::from(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"));
        let mut root = manifest.as_path();
        while let Some(parent) = root.parent() {
            if parent.join("config").join("pins.toml").is_file() {
                return parent.join("config").join("pins.toml");
            }
            root = parent;
        }
        manifest.join("../../config/pins.toml")
    }
    //! Desktop application state.
    //!
    //! The GPUI layer owns presentation only. It never reaches into the native
    //! worker: it renders immutable snapshots that the session supervisor
    //! publishes.
    
    use lotus_session::{SessionId, SessionState};
    use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
    
    /// Summary of one emulator instance, as shown in the instance list.
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    pub struct SessionSummary {
        /// Session identifier.
        pub id: String,
        /// Current lifecycle state.
        pub state: SessionState,
        /// Console model the session emulates.
        pub model: String,
        /// Render backend the session requested.
        pub renderer: String,
    }
    
    /// State of the desktop application.
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Default, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    pub struct LotusUiState {
        /// Sessions known to the supervisor.
        pub sessions: Vec<SessionSummary>,
        /// Identifier of the selected session.
        pub selected: Option<String>,
        /// Worker protocol version the UI was built against.
        pub protocol_version: String,
    }
    
    impl LotusUiState {
        /// Create the initial state.
        pub fn new() -> Self {
            Self {
                sessions: Vec::new(),
                selected: None,
                protocol_version: lotus_protocol::protocol_id(),
            }
        }
    
        /// Summary of a session.
        pub fn summary(
            id: SessionId,
            state: SessionState,
            model: impl Into<String>,
            renderer: impl Into<String>,
        ) -> SessionSummary {
            SessionSummary {
                id: id.to_string(),
                state,
                model: model.into(),
                renderer: renderer.into(),
            }
        }
    
        /// Select a session by identifier.
        pub fn select(&mut self, id: &str) {
            if self.sessions.iter().any(|session| session.id == id) {
                self.selected = Some(id.to_string());
            }
        }
    
        /// Summary of the selected session.
        pub fn selected_session(&self) -> Option<&SessionSummary> {
            let selected = self.selected.as_ref()?;
            self.sessions.iter().find(|session| &session.id == selected)
        }
    }
    
    #[cfg(test)]
    mod tests {
        use super::*;
    
        #[test]
        fn selection_requires_a_known_session() {
            let mut state = LotusUiState::new();
            state.select("session-00000000000000000000000000000001");
            assert!(state.selected.is_none());
    
            state.sessions.push(SessionSummary {
                id: "session-1".to_string(),
                state: SessionState::Idle,
                model: "old3ds".to_string(),
                renderer: "software".to_string(),
            });
            state.select("session-1");
            assert_eq!(state.selected.as_deref(), Some("session-1"));
            assert!(state.selected_session().is_some());
        }
    
        #[test]
        fn protocol_version_is_reported() {
            assert_eq!(LotusUiState::new().protocol_version, "1.0");
        }
    }
    # 04 — Building the native Azahar worker (Option B)
    
    **Scope:** the actual native Azahar core. Explicitly **not** `src/citra_libretro`. The goal is a small, maintainable C++ executable with a portable IPC boundary, not an FFI binding of every C++ class into Rust.
    
    ## Source facts verified against current Azahar master (2026-11-15)
    
    - `src/core/core.cpp` declares `Core::System System::s_instance` and contains `System::RunLoop`, `Load`, `SingleStep`, `ProcessPendingWork`, `ProcessPendingWorkUntil` and `NotifyPendingWork`.
    - `src/core/core.h` exposes `Load(Frontend::EmuWindow&, filepath, secondary_window)`, `RunLoop(bool tight_loop=true)`, `SingleStep`, `RequestShutdown`, `Memory`, `Kernel`, `GPU`, `CoreTiming`.
    - `src/core/frontend/emu_window.h`: `WindowSystemType::Headless`; virtual `PollEvents`; `CreateSharedContext`; window info with `render_surface=nullptr`; touch methods; framebuffer layout and context lifecycle.
    - `src/video_core/renderer_vulkan/vk_platform.cpp` recognizes headless window type. **Does not guarantee end-to-end GPU screenshots or offscreen output**; test it.
    - `src/core/core_timing.cpp` schedules events and virtual CPU timers, with configurable tick base and CPU clock percentage.
    - `src/video_core/gpu.cpp`: `GPU::Execute` receives GSP requests, `SubmitCmdList` triggers the PICA command processor, VBlank events are registered, DMA/display transfers are handled.
    - `src/video_core/pica/pica_core.cpp`: `PicaCore` owns internal registers, shader engine, geometry pipeline, trigger-draw handling.
    - `src/core/rpc/rpc_server.cpp`: existing RPC includes memory access and screenshots; `src/core/rpc/udp_server.cpp` uses a fixed UDP port `45987` (unsuitable as-is for independent workers).
    - `src/CMakeLists.txt` adds core, video, audio, network and input libraries, then Qt/Libretro by options. `src/core/CMakeLists.txt` builds `citra_core`.
    
    These are integration leads, not claims that an `EmuWindow` subclass can be implemented without further missing interfaces.
    
    ## Native worker responsibilities
    
    1. Parse per-worker config from supervisor: root dir, file path, selected graphics backend, initial clock/3DS model, debug mode, IPC endpoint, requested test determinism, audio on/off.
    2. Create native file/path environment and register frontend applets, microphone/image callbacks, video and input bridges.
    3. Initialize `Core::System::GetInstance()`; `Load` selected executable; report structured error/status.
    4. Own the *single* emulation thread. Execute `RunLoop(true)` for running mode; `SingleStep()` only when correct CPU stepping semantics are confirmed.
    5. Drain only explicitly allowed control requests at `ProcessPendingWork` safe points; allow quiescent pause commands to be applied even when frame limiting is sleeping.
    6. Route screen/audio from backend to bounded shared-memory/output queues; never block the emulation thread indefinitely waiting on a slow GPUI client.
    7. On exit, flush/close storage, complete or reject pending control messages, stop video/audio threads, destroy renderer, then unload and report final state.
    
    ## First implementation spike: choose software renderer
    
    A software renderer avoids the GPU surface and Vulkan readback uncertainties during earliest UI bring-up. Disable Qt; compile worker target with video software backend and required dependencies. Once images+input+audio work, add offscreen Vulkan.
    
    **Build configuration sketch (must be validated on chosen source SHA):**
    
    ```bash
    cmake -S vendor/azahar -B build/azahar-worker \
      -DENABLE_QT=OFF \
      -DENABLE_LIBRETRO=OFF \
      -DENABLE_CTR_WORKER=ON \
      -DENABLE_SOFTWARE_RENDERER=ON \
      -DENABLE_VULKAN=ON \
      -DENABLE_SCRIPTING=OFF \
      -DENABLE_WEB_SERVICE=OFF \
      -DENABLE_ROOM=OFF \
      -DENABLE_ROOM_STANDALONE=OFF
    cmake --build build/azahar-worker --target ctr-worker --config RelWithDebInfo
    ```
    
    `ENABLE_CTR_WORKER` and `ctr-worker` are **new proposed names** and do not exist upstream yet. `RelWithDebInfo` handling and toolchain configuration depend on the chosen CMake generator. Some existing conditionals are tied to `ENABLE_QT`; inventory and remove accidental dependencies before declaring `Qt OFF` functional. Keep stock Azahar build independently testable.
    
    ## CMake changes (integration branch)
    
    Minimal, additive changes:
    
    - Root `CMakeLists.txt`: `option(ENABLE_CTR_WORKER "Build external emulation worker" OFF)`, set any mutual exclusions deliberately; don't repurpose Libretro flags.
    - `src/CMakeLists.txt`: `if(ENABLE_CTR_WORKER) add_subdirectory(ctr_worker) endif()` near other frontend targets.
    - `src/ctr_worker/CMakeLists.txt`: add executable with `worker_main.cpp`, `worker_frontend.cpp`, `worker_control.cpp`, `worker_capture.cpp`, `worker_input.cpp`, `worker_audio.cpp`, `worker_storage.cpp`. Link existing Azahar `citra_core`, `video_core`, `audio_core`, other dependencies verified by target graph. Do **not** duplicate core source compilation.
    - Explicitly choose a toolchain configuration and avoid linking existing Qt application objects. Keep native worker code in a small directory, with platform-specific socket/shared-memory code isolated.
    
    A hard requirement is that `ENABLE_CTR_WORKER=OFF` leaves upstream build behavior unchanged.
    
    ## Frontend construction
    
    Create `WorkerEmuWindow final : public Frontend::EmuWindow` with:
    - `WindowSystemInfo` set to `Headless` and null surface initially.
    - `PollEvents` forwards input/config messages gathered by the worker (no native GUI event loop).
    - `GetFramebufferLayout` uses an explicit top/bottom layout; touch coordinates are mapped from GPUI to bottom-screen pixel coordinates and forwarded to `TouchPressed/Moved/Released`.
    - `CreateSharedContext` initially returns null where supported; if renderer requires one, implement a renderer-specific offscreen context, not a fake pointer.
    - Configure min/layout sizes before `Core::System::Load` and keep their lifetime valid through shutdown.
    - Implement or register the frontend software keyboard, Mii selector and image/audio input services where games request them; don't silently treat all applets as successful. For headless tests, return a clear `NEEDS_UI_INTERACTION` event with timeout/fallback policy.
    
    Investigate the actual existing `citra_qt` and SDL-like frontend implementation for callbacks and ownership; `EmuWindow` alone doesn't cover every service.
    
    ## Initial running loop and command queue
    
    **Design pseudocode (not drop-in Azahar code):**
    
    ```cpp
    while (!shutdown_requested) {
        drain_nonblocking_control_messages();  // queues only
        switch (state) {
          case Running:
            result = system.RunLoop(true);
            break;
          case Paused:
            system.ProcessPendingWork();  // including debugger commands
            wait_on_control_condition_with_timeout();
            continue;
          case StepPending:
            result = run_step_for_selected_core_or_stop_with_error();
            state = Paused;
            break;
        }
        publish_run_result_if_needed(result);
        if (fatal(result)) break;
    }
    ```
    
    `SingleStep()` currently executes `RunLoop(false)`, which may interact with **all** CPU cores and scheduling. Do not label that 'step selected ARM11 core by exactly one instruction' until verified; add per-thread/per-core step semantics on experimental branch with tests. Never enter `RunLoop` recursively from a debugger callback. Add a safe-point queue to `ProcessPendingWork`, and use `NotifyPendingWork()` to wake the core on requests. Make pending requests cancellable on shutdown.
    
    ## Read/write semantics
    
    A memory read must specify `process_id`, `address_space`, `guest_address`, `length`, `consistency`. Validate range and permissions, avoid blindly copying virtual pointers into host buffers; use Azahar's `MemorySystem` facilities and return a typed fault, unmapped range or permission failure. GPU-backed pages may require a synchronized rasterizer flush to reflect what the CPU would observe; a pure inspector read should not secretly cause guest-visible writes or corrupt renderer caches.
    
    A write must also identify the process/space and note side effects: JIT invalidation if executable code changes, rasterizer cache invalidation for altered graphics resources, debugger-visible mutation provenance and a changed state epoch. Disable writes during uncommitted replay checkpoints.
    
    ## Frame emission
    
    - Software path: access the **final top/bottom screen images** after relevant display/layout transforms. Prefer raw native screen buffers over composited window captures; record geometry, pixel format, orientation, eye selection, crop and original guest framebuffer address.
    - Vulkan path: use an offscreen target supported by selected backend; wait for submission completion before readback or handoff; never assume `Headless` automatically presents usable images.
    - Ring buffer: at least 3 slots, slot generation/sequence, writer marks `WRITING` then `READY` with release/acquire synchronization; consumer owns a lease or copies before the writer reuses it.
    - Policy: UI may skip intermediate frames; capture/test mode must either reliably collect requested frames or return explicit dropped-frame counts. Do not silently switch the emulated game into a different clock speed to satisfy the UI.
    
    ## Audio and input
    
    - Input: make worker input atomic per emulated sampling boundary; external script has exclusive ownership, no simultaneous live controller events. Map native buttons and touch explicitly; normal gameplay can accept host timestamps but replay uses guest event boundaries.
    - Audio: start with existing Azahar audio stream to a per-worker ring; UI/supervisor mixes host playback streams or selects active one. Headless workers can discard playback but preserve emulated DSP execution and track underruns.
    - Microphone/camera/system keyboards: provide deterministic fixtures for tests; interactive mode can request user values. Do not pretend missing sensors exist.
    
    ## Storage and settings
    
    Azahar uses settings and utility globals, including `Settings::values` and file-path helpers. Before launching a worker, set its user directory **before initialization**, and explicitly override any application-global data/cache paths. Identify every file-writing path (logs, saves, shader cache, texture packs, archive caches, firmware, cheats, screenshots, temporary files). Reject two workers sharing writable roots by default.
    
    ## Existing RPC and GDB
    
    Existing Azahar RPC is an implementation reference, not a server to expose unchanged. It binds UDP `45987`, so multiple workers would collide and it may allow unsafe access without consistent synchronization. Initial worker build should disable it and use our authenticated local IPC. Retain GDB functionality through a per-worker configurable endpoint if needed; account for its core safe-point interactions. A direct internal debugger interface is better than layering MCP atop UDP packets.
    
    ## Technical risks and explicit tests
    
    | Risk | Test / mitigation |
    |---|---|
    | Qt-only code hidden in core path | Build `ENABLE_QT=OFF`, link native worker, launch homebrew |
    | `Headless` lacks Vulkan output capture | Software first, offscreen Vulkan spike, screenshots compared |
    | `ProcessPendingWork` reentrancy/races | Concurrent control storm, pause/resume while sleeping, TSAN where possible |
    | `SingleStep` semantics differ from request | Assert per-core PC/instruction behavior with two threads |
    | IPC call blocks emulation indefinitely | Deadlines and bounded queues, cancellation tests |
    | Audio or applet stalls headless | Synthetic fallback with explicit events; no silent green result |
    | Shader cache/shared paths corrupt | Two workers start/stop with separate roots and identical ROM |
    | Resource lifetime | Open/close/reload loop, multiple sessions, forced worker kill |
    | Performance effect of debug hooks | A/B uninstrumented vs inactive-hook vs active-trace runs |
    
    ## Invariants for merge into integration
    
    No new Rust UI dependency, no new default network listener, no changed GPU timing, no permanent trace allocations on the critical path, no change to stock Azahar frontend when worker option is OFF. All changes must have an explicit upstream behavior comparison.

    //! Worker process lifecycle and session isolation.
    //!
    //! One emulator instance is one OS process running the native Azahar worker.
    //! The session manager owns those processes, their private storage roots and
    //! their state. It never links against `Core::System` and it never lets a
    //! worker failure take down the application or a sibling instance.
    
    pub mod storage;
    pub mod worker;
    
    pub use storage::StorageLayout;
    pub use worker::{WorkerFlavor, WorkerLaunchError, WorkerProcess, WorkerSpec};
    
    use lotus_protocol::capabilities::ConsoleModel;
    use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
    use std::collections::BTreeMap;
    use std::path::PathBuf;
    
    /// Identifier of a single emulator instance.
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, PartialOrd, Ord)]
    pub struct SessionId(pub u128);
    
    impl std::fmt::Display for SessionId {
        fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
            write!(f, "session-{:032x}", self.0)
        }
    }
    
    /// Lifecycle state of a session.
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]
    pub enum SessionState {
        /// Created, worker not started yet.
        Created,
        /// Worker running, content not loaded.
        Idle,
        /// Content loaded, emulation running.
        Running,
        /// Content loaded, emulation paused at a safe point.
        Paused,
        /// Worker exited normally.
        Stopped,
        /// Worker exited unexpectedly.
        Crashed,
    }
    
    impl SessionState {
        /// Whether the session can still issue emulation commands.
        pub fn is_active(&self) -> bool {
            matches!(
                self,
                SessionState::Idle | SessionState::Running | SessionState::Paused
            )
        }
    }
    
    /// Configuration of a session.
    ///
    /// Every field that affects execution must be recorded in a run manifest so
    /// that a result can be reproduced from a known configuration.
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    pub struct SessionConfig {
        /// Emulated console model.
        pub model: ConsoleModel,
        /// Render backend requested from the worker.
        pub renderer: String,
        /// Azahar branch flavour the worker was built from.
        pub worker_flavor: WorkerFlavor,
        /// Initial virtual tick value for deterministic runs.
        pub deterministic_initial_ticks: Option<u64>,
        /// Where the session keeps its private storage.
        pub storage_root: PathBuf,
        /// Free-form run parameters.
        pub parameters: BTreeMap<String, String>,
    }
    
    impl SessionConfig {
        /// Create a configuration with defaults for everything but the storage root.
        pub fn new(storage_root: impl Into<PathBuf>) -> Self {
            Self {
                model: ConsoleModel::Old3ds,
                renderer: "software".to_string(),
                worker_flavor: WorkerFlavor::Integration,
                deterministic_initial_ticks: None,
                storage_root: storage_root.into(),
                parameters: BTreeMap::new(),
            }
        }
    }
    
    /// A live session: its worker process, its state and its storage.
    #[derive(Debug)]
    pub struct Session {
        /// Session identifier.
        pub id: SessionId,
        /// Configuration the session was created with.
        pub config: SessionConfig,
        /// Private storage layout for this session.
        pub storage: StorageLayout,
        /// Worker process, absent before the worker is started.
        pub worker: Option<WorkerProcess>,
        /// Current lifecycle state.
        pub state: SessionState,
    }
    
    impl Session {
        /// Create a session with a fresh, isolated storage layout.
        pub fn new(id: SessionId, config: SessionConfig) -> std::io::Result<Self> {
            let storage = StorageLayout::create(&config.storage_root, id)?;
            Ok(Self {
                id,
                config,
                storage,
                worker: None,
                state: SessionState::Created,
            })
        }
    
        /// Whether the session is still usable.
        pub fn is_active(&self) -> bool {
            self.state.is_active()
        }
    }
    
    /// Registry of sessions owned by this application.
    #[derive(Debug, Default)]
    pub struct SessionManager {
        sessions: BTreeMap<SessionId, Session>,
    }
    
    impl SessionManager {
        /// Create an empty manager.
        pub fn new() -> Self {
            Self::default()
        }
    
        /// Create and register a session.
        pub fn create(&mut self, config: SessionConfig) -> std::io::Result<SessionId> {
            let id = SessionId(next_session_id());
            let session = Session::new(id, config)?;
            self.sessions.insert(id, session);
            Ok(id)
        }
    
        /// Look up a session.
        pub fn get(&self, id: &SessionId) -> Option<&Session> {
            self.sessions.get(id)
        }
    
        /// Look up a session for mutation.
        pub fn get_mut(&mut self, id: &SessionId) -> Option<&mut Session> {
            self.sessions.get_mut(id)
        }
    
        /// Identifiers of all registered sessions.
        pub fn ids(&self) -> Vec<SessionId> {
            self.sessions.keys().copied().collect()
        }
    
        /// Number of registered sessions.
        pub fn len(&self) -> usize {
            self.sessions.len()
        }
    
        /// Whether no session is registered.
        pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
            self.sessions.is_empty()
        }
    
        /// Remove a session and stop its worker.
        pub fn shutdown(&mut self, id: &SessionId) -> Option<Session> {
            let mut session = self.sessions.remove(id)?;
            if let Some(mut worker) = session.worker.take() {
                worker.terminate();
            }
            session.state = SessionState::Stopped;
            Some(session)
        }
    }
    
    /// Monotonic session counter mixed with the process id.
    fn next_session_id() -> u128 {
        use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};
        static COUNTER: AtomicU64 = AtomicU64::new(1);
        let counter = COUNTER.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
        let pid = std::process::id() as u128;
        (pid << 64) | counter as u128
    }

        fn temp_root(name: &str) -> PathBuf {
            let dir =
                std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("lotus-session-test-{name}-{}", std::process::id()));
            let _ = std::fs::remove_dir_all(&dir);
            dir
        }
    
        #[test]
        fn sessions_get_isolated_storage() {
            let root = temp_root("isolated");
            let mut manager = SessionManager::new();
            let a = manager.create(SessionConfig::new(root.join("a"))).unwrap();
            let b = manager.create(SessionConfig::new(root.join("b"))).unwrap();
    
            let storage_a = manager.get(&a).unwrap().storage.root();
            let storage_b = manager.get(&b).unwrap().storage.root();
            assert_ne!(storage_a, storage_b);
            assert!(storage_a.is_dir());
            assert!(storage_b.is_dir());
            let _ = std::fs::remove_dir_all(&root);
        }
    
        #[test]
        fn shutdown_stops_the_session() {
            let root = temp_root("shutdown");
            let mut manager = SessionManager::new();
            let id = manager.create(SessionConfig::new(root.join("s"))).unwrap();
            assert_eq!(manager.len(), 1);
            let session = manager.shutdown(&id).unwrap();
            assert_eq!(session.state, SessionState::Stopped);
            assert!(manager.is_empty());
            let _ = std::fs::remove_dir_all(&root);

            let a = manager.create(SessionConfig::new(root.join("a"))).unwrap();
            let b = manager.create(SessionConfig::new(root.join("b"))).unwrap();
            assert_ne!(a, b);
            let _ = std::fs::remove_dir_all(&root);

    //! Versioned worker protocol types.
    //!
    //! The protocol version is independent of the Azahar revision a worker was
    //! built from. Every cross-process integer is fixed width and every struct
    //! that crosses the IPC boundary is plain data: no `std::string`, no
    //! `std::vector`, no host pointers and no `Core::System` internals.
    
    pub mod capabilities;
    pub mod envelope;
    pub mod error;
    pub mod ffi;
    
    /// Major protocol version. A worker that speaks a different major version is
    /// refused at handshake instead of being coerced.
    pub const PROTOCOL_VERSION_MAJOR: u16 = 1;
    
    /// Minor protocol version. Minor bumps are additive only.
    pub const PROTOCOL_VERSION_MINOR: u16 = 0;
    
    /// Lowest minor version this build can talk to.
    ///
    /// Bumping this is a breaking change for old peers and needs a protocol
    /// migration note.
    pub const MIN_SUPPORTED_MINOR: u16 = 0;
    
    /// The minimum peer version, packed the same way as [`peer_version`].
    const MIN_SUPPORTED_VERSION: u32 =
        ((PROTOCOL_VERSION_MAJOR as u32) << 16) | (MIN_SUPPORTED_MINOR as u32);
    
    /// Pack a major and minor version into a single comparable number.
    const fn peer_version(major: u16, minor: u16) -> u32 {
        ((major as u32) << 16) | (minor as u32)
    }
    
    /// Human readable protocol identifier, e.g. `"1.0"`.
    pub fn protocol_id() -> String {
        format!("{PROTOCOL_VERSION_MAJOR}.{PROTOCOL_VERSION_MINOR}")
    }
    
    /// Check that a peer speaking `peer_major`.`peer_minor` is compatible.
    ///
    /// The major version must match exactly. A peer with a *higher* minor
    /// version is accepted: unknown optional fields may be ignored. A peer with a
    /// *lower* minor version is accepted only when this build does not require
    /// any field that the peer may be missing, which is what
    /// [`MIN_SUPPORTED_MINOR`] expresses.
    pub fn is_compatible(peer_major: u16, peer_minor: u16) -> bool {
        peer_major == PROTOCOL_VERSION_MAJOR
            && peer_version(peer_major, peer_minor) >= MIN_SUPPORTED_VERSION
    }
    
    #[cfg(test)]
    mod tests {
        use super::*;
    
        #[test]
        fn protocol_id_is_major_minor() {
            assert_eq!(protocol_id(), "1.0");
        }
    
        #[test]
        fn same_major_is_compatible() {
            assert!(is_compatible(1, 0));
        }
    
        #[test]
        fn newer_minor_is_compatible() {
            assert!(is_compatible(1, 7));
        }
    
        #[test]
        fn different_major_is_incompatible() {
            assert!(!is_compatible(0, 9));
            assert!(!is_compatible(2, 0));
        }
    
        #[test]
        fn the_minimum_supported_minor_is_accepted() {
            assert!(is_compatible(1, MIN_SUPPORTED_MINOR));
        }
    }

    //!
    //! Capabilities are reported by the worker at handshake. They must be
