    //! protocol crate would like the worker to support.
    
    use std::collections::BTreeMap;
    
    use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
    
    /// Console model a worker emulates.
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]
    pub enum ConsoleModel {
        /// Original 2011 Nintendo 3DS.
        Old3ds,
        /// New Nintendo 3DS.
        New3ds,
    }
    
    /// Graphics backend a worker was built with.
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]
    pub enum RenderBackend {
        /// CPU based renderer.
        Software,
        /// Vulkan based renderer.
        Vulkan,
        /// OpenGL based renderer.
        Opengl,
    }
    
    /// Optional worker features.
    ///
    /// Every field is set from a build flag or a runtime probe. A feature that was
    /// not compiled in must be reported as `false`, never as "probably works".
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, Default, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]
    pub struct Features {
        /// CPU debugging: breakpoints, stepping, register inspection.
        pub cpu_debug: bool,
        /// GPU draw capture and shader state inspection.
        pub gpu_draw_snapshot: bool,
        /// Firmware boot without a flashback payload.
        pub firmware_boot: bool,
        /// Worker runs without a window system.
        pub headless: bool,
    }
    
    /// Capabilities advertised by a worker.
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    pub struct Capabilities {
        /// Protocol identifier, e.g. `"1.0"`.
        pub protocol: String,
        /// Azahar revision the worker was built from.
        pub worker_sha: String,
        /// Emulated console model.
        pub model: ConsoleModel,
        /// Compiled in render backends.
        pub render_backends: Vec<RenderBackend>,
        /// Runtime feature flags.
        pub features: Features,
        /// Largest single memory read accepted.
        pub max_memory_read_bytes: u64,
        /// Largest trace held in memory.
        pub max_trace_bytes: u64,
    }
    
    impl Capabilities {
        /// Default limits used by the reference worker.
        pub const DEFAULT_MAX_MEMORY_READ_BYTES: u64 = 1024 * 1024;
        /// Default trace budget used by the reference worker.
        pub const DEFAULT_MAX_TRACE_BYTES: u64 = 512 * 1024 * 1024;
    
        /// Whether the worker advertises a given render backend.
        pub fn supports_backend(&self, backend: RenderBackend) -> bool {
            self.render_backends.contains(&backend)
        }
    
        /// Whether the worker advertises a named feature.
        pub fn supports_feature(&self, feature: &str) -> bool {
            match feature {
                "cpu_debug" => self.features.cpu_debug,
                "gpu_draw_snapshot" => self.features.gpu_draw_snapshot,
                "firmware_boot" => self.features.firmware_boot,
                "headless" => self.features.headless,
                _ => false,
            }
        }
    }
    
    /// Free-form feature map used by tooling that wants a stable, name keyed view.
    pub type FeatureMap = BTreeMap<String, bool>;

    //! Lotus desktop application.

    /// Root view of the Lotus window.

    impl Render for LotusWindow {
        fn render(&mut self, _window: &mut Window, _cx: &mut Context<Self>) -> impl IntoElement {
            let header = div()
                .flex()
                .items_center()
                .justify_between()
                .w_full()
                .h(px(40.0))
                .px_4()
                .border_b_1()
                .border_color(rgb(0x3a3a3a))
                .child("Lotus")
                .child(format!("worker protocol {}", self.state.protocol_version));
    
            let instances = if self.state.sessions.is_empty() {
                div()
                    .flex_1()
                    .p_4()
                    .text_sm()
                    .text_color(rgb(0x9a9a9a))
                    .child("No emulator instances. Start a worker to begin.")
            } else {
                div()
                    .flex_1()
                    .flex_col()
                    .p_2()
                    .gap_1()
                    .children(self.state.sessions.iter().map(instance_row))
            };
    
            let screens = div()
                .flex()
                .flex_col()
                .flex_1()
                .items_center()
                .justify_center()
                .gap_2()
                .border_l_1()
                .border_color(rgb(0x3a3a3a))
                .child(
                    div()
                        .w(px(400.0))
                        .h(px(240.0))
                        .rounded_md()
                        .border_1()
                        .border_color(rgb(0x3a3a3a))
                        .child("top screen"),
                )
                .child(
                    div()
                        .w(px(320.0))
                        .h(px(240.0))
                        .rounded_md()
                        .border_1()
                        .border_color(rgb(0x3a3a3a))
                        .child("bottom screen"),
                );
    
            div()
                .flex()
                .flex_col()
                .size_full()
                .bg(rgb(0x1e1e1e))
                .text_color(rgb(0xe6e6e6))
                .child(header)
                .child(
                    div()
                        .flex()
                        .flex_1()
                        .w_full()
                        .child(instances)
                        .child(screens),
                )
        }
    }
    
    /// One row of the instance list.
    fn instance_row(session: &SessionSummary) -> impl IntoElement {

            .flex()
            .items_center()
            .justify_between()

    fn main() {
        application().run(|cx: &mut App| {
            let bounds = Bounds::centered(None, size(px(1024.0), px(768.0)), cx);
    
            cx.open_window(
                WindowOptions {
                    window_bounds: Some(WindowBounds::Windowed(bounds)),
                    ..Default::default()
                },
                |_, cx| {
                    cx.new(|_| LotusWindow {
                        state: LotusUiState::new(),

                },
            )
            .expect("cannot open the Lotus window");

    # Lotus native Azahar worker.
    #
    # The worker is a separate OS process that runs the pinned Azahar core behind
    # a minimal frontend. It knows nothing about GPUI, MCP or agents.
    #
    # One configured build directory per Azahar branch. Never build the
    # integration and the experimental branch with the same CMake cache.
    #
    #   cmake -S workers/azahar -B build/azahar-integration \
    #         -DLOTUS_AZAHAR_ROOT=$PWD/vendor/azahar \
    #         -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
    #   cmake --build build/azahar-integration
    #
    # Without LOTUS_AZAHAR_ROOT the worker builds as a protocol stub that prints
    # its handshake and exits. That stub is useful to check the ABI and the
    # header, and it is not an emulator.
    
    cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25)
    project(lotus-azahar-worker LANGUAGES CXX)
    
    set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)
    set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
    set(CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS ON)
    
    add_executable(lotus-worker
        src/worker_main.cpp
    )
    
    target_include_directories(lotus-worker PRIVATE
        ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include
    )
    
    if(DEFINED LOTUS_AZAHAR_ROOT AND EXISTS "${LOTUS_AZAHAR_ROOT}/CMakeLists.txt")
        message(STATUS "Building the worker against Azahar at ${LOTUS_AZAHAR_ROOT}")
        add_subdirectory(${LOTUS_AZAHAR_ROOT} ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/azahar EXCLUDE_FROM_ALL)
        target_compile_definitions(lotus-worker PRIVATE LOTUS_WITH_AZAHAR)
        # The Azahar core target is named by its own build; the integration
        # branch wires the real target here.
        if(TARGET citra_core)
            target_link_libraries(lotus-worker PRIVATE citra_core)
        else()
            message(WARNING "Azahar was added, but the core target name has not been pinned yet. "
                            "The worker will be built without the native core.")
        endif()
    else()
        message(STATUS "LOTUS_AZAHAR_ROOT is not set: building the protocol stub only")
    endif()

    # and >=3.25 required to make LTO work on Android.

    # 06 — IPC, session protocol, safe points and lifecycle
    
    ## Purpose
    
    The IPC contract must survive Azahar upgrades, debug feature additions, replacement of the C++ worker and future non-Azahar execution engines. Treat IPC as a *product boundary*, not an easy way to expose Azahar classes.
    
    ## Transport
    
    - Windows: private named pipe by default. Linux/macOS: Unix-domain socket. Authenticate via OS filesystem/pipe permissions and a supervisor-created random capability token in handshake; token is a defense-in-depth measure, not a substitute for OS access rules.
    - Frame format: length-delimited binary Protocol Buffers (proposal), explicit max message size, request ID, session ID, epoch, protocol major/minor, payload, response status; async events have monotonically increasing per-worker sequence.
    - Reject oversized frames before allocating memory; no unbounded recursion/arrays or untrusted length fields. Define a maximum for every request, including reads, captures and event batches.
    - No host-facing public TCP/UDP listener in normal mode. If remote control is added later, require explicit opt-in, TLS, strong authentication and per-session authorization.
    
    ## Proposed envelope
    
    ```text
    Request { version, request_id, session_id, expected_epoch,
              deadline_ms, method, body }
    Reply   { version, request_id, session_id, actual_epoch,
              status, body, error_detail }
    Event   { version, session_id, epoch, seq, guest_tick?,
              host_ns?, kind, body }
    ```
    
    Schema fields are **proposals**, not verified Azahar wire structures. Maintain machine-readable schema in `specs/` and generate Rust/C++ code with reproducible tools. C ABI and public RPC structs use fixed-width types; no cross-language C++ STL objects.
    
    ### Critical statuses
    
    `OK`, `INVALID_ARGUMENT`, `UNSUPPORTED`, `NOT_READY`, `NOT_PAUSED`, `BUSY`, `TIMEOUT`, `STALE_EPOCH`, `UNMAPPED`, `PERMISSION_DENIED`, `RESOURCE_LIMIT`, `INCONSISTENT_SNAPSHOT`, `WORKER_EXITED`, `INTERNAL`. Do not answer `OK` because a request was queued; distinguish `ACCEPTED` (pending) from committed completion.
    
    ## Handshake example
    
    ```
    client -> worker: HELLO(protocol=1.0, session_uuid, nonce,
                            requested_features=[cpu_debug,gpu_capture,frame_ring])
    worker -> client: CAPABILITIES(protocol=1.0, worker_sha,
                            azahar_sha, model=old3ds,
                            backends=[software,vulkan], max_read=..., ...)
    client -> worker: CONFIGURE(instance_root, output_buffers, audio_policy, deterministic_seed)
    worker -> client: READY(epoch=1)
    ```
    
    Every session advertises **actual** capabilities. Never promise features based solely on the branch name. Handshake failure cannot leave a live orphan worker or a partially writable save root.
    
    ## Epoch and sequencing
    
    Increment state epoch after load, reset, restore/rewind or any operation invalidating address-space/resource identity. A request referencing an older epoch is rejected, except immutable historical-capture reads that specify an artifact ID. GPU draw/resource references include `(epoch, frame_seq, draw_seq)`; a plain register index is not sufficient context to reconstruct past state.
    
    All mutating requests (memory writes, breaks, input injection, clock changes) are serialized through the emulation thread. Query commands may use a published immutable snapshot or schedule a safe-point read.
    
    ## Safe-point queue
    
    Existing Azahar's `System::ProcessPendingWork()` runs GDB and scripting operations on the emulation thread and is invoked between slices/while waiting in the frame limiter. Add the worker's request queue here or a similarly clearly defined place; follow the same wakeup strategy via `NotifyPendingWork()` when new work arrives. Source: https://github.com/azahar-emu/azahar/blob/master/src/core/core.cpp
    
    Rules:
    1. The IPC receiving thread **does not read mutable `Core::System`, GPU or kernel objects directly**.
    2. It validates framing, enqueue bounded command, returns pending/request ID if long-running.
    3. The emulation thread reaches a safe point, validates epoch and required run state, performs operation, emits final completion.
    4. Screenshot/GPU readback may finish on a renderer worker; the control operation remains pending until the requested consistency contract is met.
    5. Safe-point operations have a budget; a massive memory read runs in bounded chunks or deliberately stops emulation. Long tasks should never leave a half-applied guest mutation.
    6. A pause request transitions through `PAUSING`, then completes only once requested CPU state is quiescent. Avoid claiming GPU is quiescent unless a separate barrier completed.
    
    ## Stepping contract
    
    Avoid ambiguous `step`. Define:
    
    - `step_cpu_instruction(core_id, thread_id?)`: exactly one retired guest instruction on the selected core/thread or return `UNSUPPORTED` if backend cannot honor it. Test against Azahar's `SingleStep()` semantics; it currently delegates to `RunLoop(false)` and is not proven to target one selected core.
    - `step_to_event(event_filter)`: stop at next selected callback or guest event; may execute arbitrary instructions.
    - `step_frame(boundary=top_vblank_start|bottom_vblank_start|presented_frame)`: explicit boundary, record skipped/duplicate presentation.
    - `run_until(breakpoint|guest_tick|frame_count|event|timeout)`: bounded by both guest goal and host timeout, with stop reason and final state.
    - `pause(mode=cpu_only|capture_consistent)`: stronger mode may wait for renderer synchronization.
    
    ## Shared-memory image ring
    
    Descriptor per ring: magic, schema, session/epoch, slot_count, width, height, stride, pixel format, screen/eye identity, handle/lifetime token. Slot metadata: atomic state, generation, sequence, guest frame seq, capture host timestamp, bytes valid, hash. Writer must never overwrite a leased slot; use bounded drop/backpressure policy. Ring reallocation increments generation, requires consumer acknowledgement and does not reuse an old OS handle while clients still reference it. Stale access becomes a typed error.
    
    Nominal 3DS native screens: top 400x240, bottom 320x240; RGB(A) output must identify stereoscopic eye. Hardware often stores rotated framebuffers; define whether published pixels are normalized to display orientation. Do not rely on shape alone.
    
    ## Control / observation surface
    
    | Method group | Commands | Minimum info returned |
    |---|---|---|
    | Session | load, run, pause, reset, stop, status | state, epoch, stop reason, config hash |
    | CPU | regs, disasm, step, breakpoints | core, thread, mode, PC, validity |
    | Memory | map, read, write, search, watch | process, space, range, epoch, errors |
    | Kernel | process/thread list, IPC trace, wait graph | IDs, scheduling/wait states, event seq |
    | GPU | external/internal regs, command lists, draw, textures, frame | draw/frame identity, capture consistency |
    | DSP | state, audio ring/underrun metrics | sample time, emulation status, backend |
    | Trace | arm, start, stop, flush, export | filters, counts, dropped, artifact hash |
    | Input | inject, set script ownership, touch | accepted boundary, effective sample tick |
    
    ## Cancellation and idempotency
    
    - `get_*` reads are idempotent with snapshot/epoch identities; live reads may differ across calls.
    - `load`, `reset`, `write_memory` and `run_until` are **not** automatically idempotent. Replayed request IDs return recorded result within a bounded retention window, not reapply mutation.
    - Cancellation interrupts waiting/pending operations and reports whether effect was already committed; cannot rewind a half-frame by fiat.
    - `stop` attempts graceful shutdown, then terminates worker at deadline; report unflushed output and preserve crash logs.
    
    ## Artifacts
    
    Export a manifest and content-addressed files, not opaque log text. `manifest.json` includes worker/branch hashes, GPUI/protocol version, game hash (not ROM bytes), model, graphics backend, selected test, input seed, time domains, capture feature flags, timestamps, dropped-event counters, storage snapshot ID and host environment. Large binary files have SHA-256 checksums and explicit schema IDs.
    
    ## Security and privacy
    
    MCP is not allowed to supply arbitrary absolute worker paths. Supervisor allocates roots under its own managed workspace; reads/writes are by object handles or normalized virtual-relative paths. Memory writes/patches and firmware access are privileged tool categories that require explicit session capabilities. Retain a local audit trail of mutating commands. Avoid collecting screenshots or saves unless requested by user/test scenario; provide retention/deletion controls.

    # 05 — GPUI desktop application: architecture, UX and rendering
    
    ## Framework contract
    
    Use Zed's **GPUI**, not Electron, a web shell or React Native. Build a Rust native app with entities/views/elements, action-driven keyboard shortcuts and async work. The `gpui_platform::application()` entrypoint chooses host platform; GPUI's own README reports Windows Win32/DirectWrite, macOS Metal (`font-kit` for glyphs), Linux Wayland/X11 options. **Pin the GPUI source commit**; the project is pre-1.0 and breaking changes are expected. Source: https://github.com/zed-industries/zed/blob/main/crates/gpui/README.md
    
    ## Application entities and data ownership
    
    ```text
    AppModel
    ├─ WorkspaceModel             open docks, tabs, saved layouts
    ├─ SessionList                worker handles + health
    │  └─ SessionViewModel        immutable latest snapshots and subscriptions
    ├─ CaptureStore               immutable capture/artifact metadata
    ├─ SymbolIndex                per-process ELF/symbol resolvers
    ├─ DebuggerModel              breakpoints, watches, focused thread, active frame
    └─ Preferences                UI / input mapping / privacy
    ```
    
    The worker never calls into GPUI. A background task reads IPC, validates message ordering/epoch, stores immutable snapshots in a bounded cache and schedules UI model changes via GPUI's thread-safe executor/context mechanisms appropriate to pinned API. Never mutate a GPUI entity from an unmanaged worker thread. Coalesce high-frequency telemetry; don't re-render the entire debugger view for every GPU register change.
    
    ## Minimum viable layout
    
    - Central document area: 3DS top/bottom images; layout presets (stacked, side-by-side, single-screen, right-eye, native-resolution view); independently zoom and pan; pixel inspection mode with nearest-neighbor sampling.
    - Left dock: sessions + launch presets, process/thread tree, breakpoints/watchpoints.
    - Right dock: registers/disassembly, memory browser, PICA state/draw details; searchable, synchronized to selected snapshot.
    - Bottom dock: structured event log, tracing status/dropped counts, scripts/test results, audio underruns, worker errors.
    - Timeline: separate lanes for CPU execution, SVCs, kernel waits, GPU command lists/draws/transfers, DSP and presentation; show guest clock and host clock independently.
    - Header: active instance/build/backend, run/pause/step controls, determinism flag, Old/New 3DS mode, timing model label.
    
    **Avoid** expensive always-live visualizations until a user opens the pane. Closed panes should not trigger costly emulator reads.
    
    ## Layout and interaction discipline
    
    - Every panel has an independent stable ID. A GPUI entity maps to an instance and snapshot ID, never a raw C++ pointer.
    - Layout persistence is versioned; unknown panel types default to safe fallback rather than losing workspace configuration.
    - All numeric addresses appear with process/core/space qualifiers (e.g. CPU virtual `PID:VA`, physical VRAM, GPU register index). Switching current process should not silently reinterpret an old address.
    - Suspended/stale snapshots are visibly marked; the UI never shows the latest register contents as though they were captured at the selected old GPU draw.
    - Provide keyboard-first navigation and palette commands. Actions should be discoverable and localizable; avoid hardcoding shortcuts in individual panels.
    - Display failures/unsupported features explicitly, e.g. `renderer does not support GPU texture capture`, not empty black screenshots.
    
    ## Native image integration: do not prematurely force zero-copy
    
    `crates/gpui/src/elements/img.rs` has `ImageSource::Render(Arc<RenderImage>)`, `ImageSource::Image` and `ImageSource::Custom` in the currently inspected source. That supports a first CPU-pixel path with decoded/allocated images. Exact `RenderImage` constructors may change: compile a 2-screen pixel-demo pinned to your chosen GPUI commit before building the worker. Source: https://github.com/zed-industries/zed/blob/main/crates/gpui/src/elements/img.rs
    
    ### Phase 1: CPU pixels
    
    1. Worker publishes normalized native-resolution RGB(A) screen images to shared-memory slots.
    2. Rust receiver validates descriptor/sequence/format and obtains or copies complete frames.
    3. Presenter creates a GPUI renderable image on demand and keeps only the newest displayable frame per active session.
    4. UI repaints at host display rate, independent of emulated frame timing; repeated frames should be permitted. Capture path uses raw frames and metadata independently of UI composition.
    5. Touch mapping uses *actual bottom-screen transform*: inverse translation/scale/rotation/zoom, clamp to native `320x240`, check pointer-down/move/release semantics, and capture the input device identity.
    
    ### Phase 2: GPU acceleration
    
    Azahar's accelerated renderer can produce Vulkan textures, while GPUI's native Windows rendering does not automatically consume them. Proof-of-concept options:
    
    - Vulkan image -> asynchronous GPU readback -> pinned CPU memory -> GPUI image. Simplest reliable progression.
    - Vulkan/D3D shared texture interop (Windows): export/import memory and synchronization objects where supported, match adapter/LUID and format, manage ownership/fences and lifetime. Needs native GPUI element/renderer extension, not just wrapping a texture handle in `img()`.
    - macOS: investigate Metal bridge/copy path separately; no assumption about Vulkan-to-Metal zero-copy.
    - Linux: investigate DMA-BUF/Vulkan interop and GPUI backend support separately.
    
    Every accelerated path must preserve a CPU fallback and report end-to-end display latency including synchronization stalls. Display throughput is not guest hardware timing.
    
    ## GPUI performance plan
    
    - Bound update rate of expensive inspectors; separate **display refresh** from **debugger state refresh**.
    - Use generation-indexed immutable snapshots and virtualized lists for instruction/event tables; never construct 100k UI rows every frame.
    - Asset lifetime: cache only bounded texture previews keyed by `(instance, frame_id, resource_id, epoch)`; evict LRU and invalidate on reset.
    - Avoid per-frame image decoding/allocations if a reusable buffer path works; benchmark the chosen GPUI image construction API.
    - Render high-cardinality timelines from compact downsampled event bins at the selected zoom; fetch full events only when selected.
    - Profile GPUI executor lag, IPC dequeue, image upload, paint time, UI stalls and presentation latency separately from native worker timings.
    
    ## Suggested app state transitions
    
    `NoSession -> Starting -> Ready -> Loading -> Running <-> Paused -> Stopping -> Stopped`. Other transitions: `Faulted`, `Disconnected`, `NeedsInput`, `Capturing`. UI action is disabled until legal. `Reset` invalidates old memory/resource generation and pending disassembly/capture requests.
    
    ## First compile-only spike
    
    1. Use pinned GPUI commit and official standalone app entrypoint.
    2. Show two dynamic generated test patterns, not a ROM.
    3. Sustain continuous frame replacement and interactive scaling for 10 minutes; check retained memory; measure CPU upload cost.
    4. Simulate 4 sessions with 2 screens each using synthetic changing frames; ensure inactive tabs don't consume similar UI resources as active ones.
    5. Draw a virtual 320x240 touch target overlay, click corners, verify inverse transform under zoom and DPI scaling.
    6. Suspend/restart frame production without dropping the UI; test worker-initiated format/size changes.
    
    This reduces risk before integrating Azahar's renderer and shows whether GPUI changes require custom Elements.
    
    ## Accessibility / quality
    
    Support keyboard navigation, visible focus, screen-reader labels where GPUI exposes them, colorblind-friendly state markers, actual selectable/copyable diagnostic text, accessible high-contrast mode. Debug panes should provide small exportable text artifacts as an alternative to screenshots.
    # Proposed worker protocol v1 (draft, NOT IMPLEMENTED)
    
    The protocol is versioned independently from Azahar branch SHA. This is a human-readable contract to drive a future machine-readable `.proto` definition after the worker spike.
    
    ## Identity and envelope
    
    ```
    Envelope:
      version_major: u16
      version_minor: u16
      request_id: u64
      session_uuid: 128-bit
      session_epoch: u64
      type: request | reply | event
      payload: tagged binary message
      max_length: enforced before decoding
    ```
    
    All cross-process integers are fixed width. Strings are UTF-8. Any guest addresses are typed and qualified by address-space + process/core ID, never host pointers. Unknown optional fields may be ignored only with compatible versioning; unknown required semantics trigger explicit failure. Replies echo request ID and record the state epoch at which they executed.
    
    ## Method skeletons
    
    ```
    CreateSession(Config) -> (SessionId, Capabilities)
    Load(SessionId, ContentHandle) -> (Epoch, ProgramIdentity, LoadResult)
    RunUntil(SessionId, Predicate, WallDeadline) -> (StopReason, StateSummary)
    Pause(SessionId, Mode) -> (StopReason, SnapshotId)
    StepInstruction(SessionId, CpuSelector) -> (StopReason, InstructionCount, SnapshotId)
    ReadMemory(SessionId, Space, ProcessId, Address, Length, Consistency) -> (Bytes|Holes, SnapshotId)
    WriteMemory(SessionId, Space, ProcessId, Address, Bytes, ExpectedEpoch) -> (NewEpochOrRevision, SideEffects)
    CaptureDraw(SessionId, FrameId, DrawId, Options) -> (ArtifactId, MissingFields)
    ConfigureTrace(SessionId, Filter, Levels, ByteBudget) -> (TraceConfigId)
    ExportTrace(SessionId, TraceId) -> (ArtifactId, Size, SHA256)
    Stop(SessionId, Deadline) -> (ExitCode, FinalStatus)
    ```
    
    ### Run predicates
    
    `frame_count`, `cpu_pc`, `svc`, `ipc_service_cmd`, `gpu_command`, `gpu_draw_id`, `guest_tick_limit`, `exception`, `wall_timeout`. Predicates must be validated and termination must be bounded.
    
    ### Snapshot visibility
    
    `cpu_safe_point`, `gpu_consistent`, `full_checkpoint`, `telemetry`. A GPU-consistent read may block on host graphics processing. A full checkpoint is refused if unsupported async work is pending. A `telemetry` read may be stale; its age is included.
    
    ### Capabilities example (illustrative)
    
    ```json
    {
      "protocol": "1.0",
      "worker_sha": "<commit>",
      "model": "old3ds",
      "render_backends": ["software", "vulkan"],
      "features": {"cpu_debug": true, "gpu_draw_snapshot": false, "firmware_boot": false},
      "max_memory_read_bytes": 1048576,
      "max_trace_bytes": 536870912
    }
    ```
    
    Example caps are **policy examples, not measured/runtime support**. Feature advertisement must be generated from actual build and runtime capability checks.
    
    ## Stream artifacts
    
    Raw screen output uses shared memory with `(generation, slot, seq, format, stride, width, height, screen, eye, epoch)`. Events use ordered worker sequence. Trace artifacts store a versioned index plus compressed chunks; chunk type IDs are distinct from serialized internal C++ structs. Export direct capture bytes only with actual user permission.
    
    ## Error semantics
    
    Never conflate submitted/accepted/finished. A long request returns a job ID and `PENDING`, followed by completion or timeout. If state mutation may have occurred but an IPC connection dropped, client must query mutation/request ID history; do not retry blindly.
    
    ## Security
    
    All endpoints local-only by default. Apply OS pipe permissions and per-session capabilities. No host shell commands or unbounded file writes. Persist audit events for debugger memory patches and external input injection.

     This document is a  style guide  for the usage of the Rust programming language
    at Google. In this context, “style” refers to more than just formatting; it
    includes guidance on API and implementation design.
    
     Rust is used in many places, including
     google3 ,
    Android, ChromeOS, Fuchsia, and Chrome, and we’d like for Rust usage at Google
    to be consistent both within and across codebases. In addition to bringing
    consistency to our Rust code, style guidance also helps establish a standard of
    quality.
    
     Background
    
     Scope
    
     The current scope of authority of the rules outlined in this guide:
    
    
        In Android, Chromium, and other codebases : This style guide has been
    developed in consultation with other codebases, and they intend to start
    applying it. These codebases may have their own rules about how strictly
    this is expected to be applied. Expect more information here as these
    codebases adopt this guide.
    
    
     Goals of the style guide
    
     By and large, we have this document for
     the same reasons we have a C++ style guide .
    
     Most style rules come from one or more of the goals listed below.
    
    
    
       Style rules should prioritize readability and maintainability over writeability
    
         We expect our code to be around for long periods of time, and we
    consider a little bit of extra effort applied during code writing to be
    worth it in the long run if the style rule improves readability.
    
    
       Style rules should favor better automation
    
         Large-Scale Changes (LSCs)
    are common at Google, and consistency helps
    make LSCs easier to carry out.
    
    
       Style rules should be consistent with the wider Rust ecosystem where possible
    
         The broader Rust ecosystem already has a pretty good amount of consistency
    in style, and we should rely on that where possible to reduce surprise and make
    it less work to learn Google’s Rust style.
    
    
       Style rules should pull their weight
    
         Every Rust developer and reviewer at Google has to keep these style rules
    in mind: as such, we should be careful to include rules that have a tangible
    benefit.
    
    
       Style rules may help avoid minor style disagreements
    
         There are many cases where reasonable people may disagree about a style, and
    we expect that disagreement to show up often on CLs. Having a style rule helps
    avoid having to rehash this each time. Rules in this category that do not have other
    benefits should be kept to a minimum.
    
    
    
    
    
    
     Follow public Rust style rules
    
     Follow the official public Rust style rules to the extent they don’t conflict
    with this style guide.
    
    
    
          Rust Style Guide
    
    
           Most code formatting conventions are enforced automatically by rustfmt.
    
    
    
          Rust API Guidelines
    
    
    
     A “conflict” would be a case where this style guide suggests a pattern that is
    discouraged, or counter to the primary encouraged pattern in the Rust style
    guide.
    
     Why does the guidance in this style guide deviate from regular Rust style rules?
    
     Most style guides have three goals: consistency, readability, and encouraging
    good API design. Regardless of the specific choices made, it helps everyone to
    have these choices made beforehand to limit bikeshedding.
    
     This style guide shares those goals, but it also has an additional goal not seen
    as often: smoothing the way for Large-Scale Changes (LSCs). Large codebases like
    many of the ones at Google occasionally need to run codebase-spanning
    refactorings that are assisted by tooling: for this to work well, the code
    should be something tooling has an easy time working with. Consistency helps for
    this, but so does having deliberate refactor-friendly patterns.
    
    
    
     Apply API design rules in context
    
     When applying rules that relate to API design, you should distinguish two types
    of code:
    
    
    
         Library code
    
    
           Intended for use by other projects (applications or other libraries).
           Solves a relatively general problem.
    
    
    
         Application code
    
    
           Intended for use in a single application.
           Solves a more specific problem.
    
    
    
    
     For  library code , style guide rules that concern API design are binding.
    
     For  application code , the rules on API design are a strong recommendation. As
    you apply them, keep in mind that since application code is written to solve a
    specific problem, it should generally favor simplicity and directness over broad
    reusability. Avoid premature generalization and abstraction; focus on what is
    required to meet the immediate need.
    
    
    
     Code organization
    
      Terminology:
    
    
    
         A  crate  is a unit of compilation. A crate always contains a nameless Rust
    module, the “root module”.
    
    
         A Rust  module  is a unit of code organization within a crate. Rust modules
    are used to control visibility of names. Modules can be nested. They can
    also be used to split code across files and directories.
    
    
    
     The following sections convey that in Chromium, it is preferable to  not  make
    use of all possibilities of splitting modules across files.
    
    
    
     Prefer small crates  [chrome]
    
     Prefer small crates in Chromium; ideally, but not necessarily, a single file
    (focusing on one abstraction). If your code can be split up into small crates,
    do so.
    
     A crate corresponds to a single  rust_static_library  (chrome) rule, which may
    contain one or more  .rs  files.
    
     Additional considerations:
    
    
    
         The root module is allowed to  re-export  public APIs from  leaf
    submodules , making submodules an implementation detail of the crate (as
    users don’t need to know about these submodules).
    
    
         This rule about small crates applies equally to crates with and without
    submodules. First, evaluate whether the APIs need to be in the same crate,
    and only then consider whether submodules could help organize the APIs.
    
    
         If you decide to use submodules, follow the
     expected file structure .
    
    
    
     Larger crates are allowed when
     trait impl coherence rules
    force multiple types and traits to be included in one library, or if you’re
    building a large foundational library.
    
     Rationale
    
     Fine-grained library targets are recommended in Chromium due to the massive size
    of our codebase, non-local effects of adding dependencies in the build graph,
    and to improve performance of parallel compilation and build caching.
    
    
    
     Use flat file layout for  rust_library  sources  [chrome]
    
     In Chromium  .rs  source files belonging to one  rust_library  (one Rust crate)
    must reside in a single directory.
    
     Don’t use subdirectories to organize files that belong to a single crate. If
    organizing one crate’s files into subdirectories feels necessary, this is a
    strong indication that the crate has grown  too large  and should
    be split.
    
     This crate layout is intentionally different from the conventional Cargo
    directory structure typically used in open-source repositories.
    
     Exception: Rust code in  //third_party  that is also built with
     Cargo  should follow the conventional Cargo
    directory structure.
    
     Rationale
    
     The approach in Chromium is driven by the following factors:
    
    
       Based on the preference for  small crates , most
     rust_library  targets will only contain one source file.
       Because of the above point, creating a directory for each  rust_library
    target would result in most directories containing only one source file.
       Multi-file  rust_library  targets should not create dedicated directories
    for submodules either; this ensures a consistent approach.
    
    
    
    
     Name source files and leaf modules after the primary user-defined item
    
     When a  leaf module  has a primary user-defined item (e.g.,  Foo ), the module
    should be named after that item (e.g.,  mod foo  and  foo.rs ).
    
     Leaf modules that are not primarily about any particular abstraction can be
    named as desired.
    
     Rationale
    
     This makes it easy to identify the content/purpose of a source file or leaf
    module at a glance.
    
    
    
     Don’t implement APIs in non-leaf modules
    
     The only items in non-leaf modules should be module declarations (not
    definitions) and  re-exports .
    
     Note that the definition of  leaf modules  allows the following sub-modules:
     mod test  and cross-language binding modules like  #[cxx::bridge] .
    
     Exceptions:
    
    
       Having a small amount of core “ties things together” implementation code in
    a non-leaf module may be fine. The goal is to not have a lot of code in
    these modules.
    
    
     Rationale
    
     This makes it easier to find things, and avoids mixing structure and contents.
    
    
    
     Don’t use glob imports
    
     Don’t use glob imports, except in the following situations where you may
    optionally do so at your own discretion:
    
    
        use super::*  for inline modules
        use enum::*  in method bodies of enums, and functions that are primarily
    dealing with that enum
        pub use submodule::*  for non-leaf modules
    
         C++ interop: Since the same namespace (in C++) is a submodule in different
    Rust crates (in Rust), you may merge the namespaces into a private copy
    using glob imports. For example:
    
             mod   absl   {
         pub   use   status  ::  absl  ::  *  ;
         pub   use   strings  ::  absl  ::  *  ;
     }
    
    
         In this hypothetical example, you can use  absl::Status  and  absl::StrCat
    from Rust, the same way you would from C++, instead of spelling them as
     status::absl::Status  and  strings::absl::StrCat .
    
         This must only be used for merging C++ namespaces, and the resulting merged
    module must not be public.
    
    
    
     If using third-party crates that encourage a prelude, it is up to the reviewer’s
    discretion to allow it.
    
     This also means that defining preludes should be avoided.
    
     Rationale
    
     Glob imports increase toil for code janitors running LSCs, and make it harder to
    know where a type comes from in contexts without xrefs.
    
    
    
     A  use  statement should import items from one module
    
     This rule corresponds to the rustfmt setting  imports_granularity = Module .
    
     Basically, there should not be any  :: ’s inside the  {..}  block of a  use
    statement. For example:
    
    
    
         use   foo  ::  Foo  ;
     use   foo  ::  bar  ::  Bar  ;
     use   foo  ::  bar  ::  Baz  ;
    
    
    
    
         use   foo  ::  Foo  ;
     use   foo  ::  bar  ::{  Bar  ,   Baz  };
    
    
    
    
         use   foo  ::{  Foo  ,   bar  ::  Bar  };
    
    
    
    
     Prefer locally-scoped trait imports
    
     Import traits within function bodies, unless the trait’s methods are used
    extensively throughout the file.
    
    
    
         fn   foo  (  x  :   u8  )   {
         // Import the trait within a function, not at the module scope.
         use   std  ::  str  ::  FromStr  ;
    
         let   string  :   String   =   x  .parse  ();
     }
    
    
    
    
     Qualify calls to top-level functions with a module name
    
     To use top-level functions defined in other modules or crates, import their
    module and call them with  modulename::functionname() . For example:
    
    
    
         use   std  ::  mem  ;
    
     let   x   =   mem  ::  transmute  (  y  );
    
    
    
    
         use   std  ::  mem  ::  transmute  ;
    
     let   x   =   transmute  (  y  );
    
    
     Exceptions:
    
    
       When importing functions with sufficiently disambiguated names, e.g.,
    functions from C++ (where it is typical to call top-level (free) functions
    directly).
    
         In Chromium, when importing functions from
     small, single-purpose first-party crates .
    
       When the module name itself is prone to collisions. For example, when the
    module name is a C++ namespace name, and multiple crates define the same
    submodules.
    
    
     Rationale
    
     Many Rust codebases consistently keep a style such that unqualified lowercase
    names are assumed local, so  foo()  can be assumed to be from the same module.
    This rule largely exists to avoid reviewer disagreements, the benefit is mostly
    consistency and a minor edge on reading code without xrefs.
    
    
    
     Type names should be imported and used unqualified
    
     By default, types and traits should be referenced in code without using their
    module path, e.g., code should use  Regex , not  regex::Regex , with a  use
    regex::Regex  at the top of the file or potentially in the relevant function.
    
     Exceptions:
    
    
       In cases where there are ambiguities, it is acceptable to directly reference
    types with common names like  io::Error . It is also acceptable to rename
    ( use std::io::Error as IoError ).
       In cases where you have a large “group” of types, e.g. the
      hir module in rustc
    which contains a large number of HIR types.
       In macros and generated code; where requiring a  use  is counterproductive.
       In code with lots of dependencies, where importing everything would lead to
    a very large import block with little benefit.
    
    
     Rationale
    
     This rule largely exists to avoid reviewer disagreements.
    
    
    
     Use the appropriate import mechanism  [chrome]
    
    
        Chrome  Use  chromium::import!() .
    
    
    
    
     Code formatting and aesthetics
    
    
    
     Use the appropriate formatting tool
    
     Use the appropriate formatting tool (e.g.,  git cl format  in Chromium).
    
     Configuration (for style guide authors)
    
     A codebase may choose to not apply the following  rustfmt  options if they care
    about building on stable and the option is unavailable on their stable Rust:
    
    
    
         Maximum of 100 columns per line:
      max_width = 100
    
    
         Usage of lowercase alphabets in hex literals ( 0xab123cdef  as opposed to
     0xAB123CDEF ):
      hex_literal_case = Lower
    
    
         Macro matcher formatting:
      format_macro_matchers = true
    
    
         Usage of escapes for invisible characters in literals. E.g., if you wish to
    have text containing a Zero-Width joiner, use  \u{200D} .
    
    
    
    
    
     Opting out of automatic formatting
    
     You may opt out of automatic formatting using  #[rustfmt::skip] , but only in
    the following situations:
    
    
        Manual alignment  – If you have a situation-specific reason to have a
    snippet of code line up in a particular way (e.g., multiple similar lines of
    code that you want to remain aligned for readability, or a
    matrix-constructing function).
        Generated code  (ideally, use a genrule instead).
    
    
     Important: Formatting should not be skipped for personal style choices.
    
    
    
     Ownership and borrowing
    
    
    
     Avoid  Rc  and  Arc
    
     Prefer unique ownership and borrowing over  Rc  and  Arc  for managing memory.
    
     Exception:
    
    
       Use  Rc  and  Arc  when the alternative ownership and borrowing structure
    would be unreasonably complex to write, understand, or maintain. This is a
    judgment call to be discussed during code review.
    
    
     Rationale
    
     Generally, Rust allows representing object graphs without using shared ownership
    smart pointers. These pointers add runtime overhead and their own unique
    complexity. Engineers coming from other languages might tend to use  Rc  and
     Arc  too quickly.
    
    
    
     Prefer borrows over deep copies
    
     Use  .clone()  when you genuinely need a deep copy of an object.
    
     Avoid using  .clone()  as a substitute for borrowing. Design code that works
    naturally with Rust’s ownership and borrowing rules. However, if the borrowing
    relationships become excessively complex,  .clone()  can be a pragmatic choice.
    
     Consider the performance needs of the code while choosing between cloning and
    borrowing.
    
     Note: This advice does not apply to cloning  Rc  or  Arc  pointers. Cloning
    reference-counted pointers does not create a deep copy, and is an expected way
    to use them.
    
     Rationale
    
     Deep copies can be expensive to make due to memory allocation and data copying.
    
    
    
     Function inputs and outputs
    
    
    
     Accept flexible references for immutable data
    
     When functions accept borrowed, immutable data, use a reference type that
    affords the most flexibility. Pass references to the data itself instead of
    references to smart pointers, containers, or wrappers.
    
    
    
    
    
    
           Use
           Instead of
           Why?
    
    
    
    
            &T
            &Box<T>
           Borrow the data inside the box
    
    
            &[T]
            &Vec<T>
           Accept any slice instead of specific containers
    
    
            &str
            &String
           Accept a string slice instead of references to owned strings
    
    
            Option<&T>
            &Option<T>
           Borrow the data inside the Option
    
    
    
    
    
    
     Exceptions:
    
    
       When expecting non-linear character data such as Rope/Cord.
    
    
     For context, see Clippy lints
      borrowed_box
    and
     ptr_arg .
    
     Rationale
    
     Accepting reference types that don’t mention specific smart pointers,
    containers, or wrappers makes functions more versatile and performant: callers
    can pass data held in a variety of ways without copying it first.
    
    
    
     Iterators vs. owned collections in return types
    
     Prefer returning iterators (either concrete types or  impl Iterator ) where
    possible over returning  Vec<T> .
    
     Note: In application c
    ✓ • 238ms

## Reasoning

**Defining protocol state fields**

## Activity

    $ @'
        //! Bounded local control messages. Large images never travel on this channel.
        use std::io::{self, Read, Write};
        
        use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
        use serde::de::DeserializeOwned;
        
        /// Maximum encoded control message, checked before allocation.
        pub const MAX_CONTROL_BYTES: u32 = 65_536;
        
        /// Commands implemented by the supervisor spike.
        #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
        #[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]
        pub enum Method {
            Hello,
            Status,
            Stop,
        }
        
        /// Completion status; OK always means completed, never merely queued.
        #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
        #[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]
        pub enum Status {
            Ok,
            InvalidArgument,
            Unsupported,
            NotReady,
            StaleEpoch,
            PermissionDenied,
        }
        
        /// Request envelope for one inherited private pipe connection.
        #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
        #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]
        pub struct Request {
            pub version_major: u16,
            pub version_minor: u16,
            pub request_id: u64,
            pub session: String,
            pub epoch: u64,
            pub method: Method,
        }
        
        /// Response envelope. Mock identity is explicit and has no emulator capabilities.
        #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
        #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]
        pub struct Reply {
            pub version_major: u16,
            pub version_minor: u16,
            pub request_id: u64,
            pub session: String,
            pub epoch: u64,
            pub status: Status,
            pub state: String,
            pub backend: String,
        }
        
        /// Encode a JSON control message behind a little-endian u32 byte count.
        pub fn encode<T: Serialize>(value: &T) -> io::Result<Vec<u8>> {
            let payload = serde_json::to_vec(value).map_err(io::Error::other)?;
            let length = u32::try_from(payload.len()).map_err(io::Error::other)?;
            validate_length(length)?;
            let mut bytes = Vec::with_capacity(payload.len() + 4);
            bytes.extend_from_slice(&length.to_le_bytes());
            bytes.extend_from_slice(&payload);
            Ok(bytes)
        }
        
        /// Reject invalid lengths before allocating payload storage.
        pub fn validate_length(length: u32) -> io::Result<()> {
            if length == 0 || length > MAX_CONTROL_BYTES {
                return Err(io::Error::new(io::ErrorKind::InvalidData, "invalid control length"));
            }
            Ok(())
        }
        
        /// Read exactly one bounded message; truncation is an error.
        pub fn read<T: DeserializeOwned>(reader: &mut impl Read) -> io::Result<T> {
            let mut prefix = [0; 4];
            reader.read_exact(&mut prefix)?;
            let length = u32::from_le_bytes(prefix);
            validate_length(length)?;
            let mut payload = vec![0; length as usize];
            reader.read_exact(&mut payload)?;
            serde_json::from_slice(&payload).map_err(io::Error::other)
        }
        
        /// Write and flush a complete message.
        pub fn write<T: Serialize>(writer: &mut impl Write, value: &T) -> io::Result<()> {
            writer.write_all(&encode(value)?)?;
            writer.flush()
        }
        
        #[cfg(test)]
        mod tests {
            use super::*;
        
            #[test]
            fn invalid_lengths_and_truncated_json_are_rejected() {
                for length in [0, MAX_CONTROL_BYTES + 1, u32::MAX] {
                    assert!(read::<Request>(&mut length.to_le_bytes().as_slice()).is_err());
                }
                assert!(read::<Request>(&mut [2, 0, 0, 0, b'{'].as_slice()).is_err());
                assert!(read::<Request>(&mut [2, 0, 0, 0, b'{', b'}'].as_slice()).is_err());
            }
        }

        //! Mock worker for process/transport acceptance; this never emulates a console.
        use std::io;
        
        use lotus_protocol::control::{self, Method, Reply, Request, Status};
        
        fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
            let mode = std::env::args().nth(1).unwrap_or_default();
            let mut input = io::stdin().lock();
            let mut output = io::stdout().lock();
            let mut identity: Option<String> = None;
            loop {
                let request: Request = control::read(&mut input)?;
                if mode == "crash" { std::process::exit(23); }
                if mode == "hang" { std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_secs(60)); continue; }
                let status = if !lotus_protocol::is_compatible(request.version_major, request.version_minor) {
                    Status::Unsupported
                } else if request.session.len() != 32 || !request.session.bytes().all(|c| c.is_ascii_hexdigit()) || request.request_id == 0 {
                    Status::InvalidArgument
                } else if identity.as_ref().is_some_and(|id| id != &request.session) {
                    Status::PermissionDenied
                } else if request.method != Method::Hello && identity.is_none() {
                    Status::NotReady
                } else if request.epoch != 1 {
                    Status::StaleEpoch
                } else {
                    if request.method == Method::Hello { identity = Some(request.session.clone()); }
                    Status::Ok
                };
                let stopped = status == Status::Ok && request.method == Method::Stop;
                let reply = Reply {
                    version_major: lotus_protocol::PROTOCOL_VERSION_MAJOR,
                    version_minor: lotus_protocol::PROTOCOL_VERSION_MINOR,
                    request_id: request.request_id,
                    session: request.session,
                    epoch: if mode == "stale" { 0 } else { 1 },
                    status,
                    state: if stopped { "stopped" } else { "idle" }.into(),
                    backend: "mock".into(),
                };
                control::write(&mut output, &reply)?;
                if stopped { return Ok(()); }
            }
        }

## Reasoning

**Preparing native polling**

## Assistant

The three Azahar worktrees now exist at the pinned upstream revision, with separate build directories planned. I’m implementing the T03 transport over inherited private pipes; it opens no listener. The supervisor checks reply identity and epoch, enforces deadlines, and reaps failed children. The mock identifies itself explicitly and advertises no emulation support.

    $ $text = Get-Content crates/session/Cargo.toml -Raw; $text = $text.Replace('tokio = { workspace = true }',''); $text.Replace('[dependencies]', '[dependencies]' + "`n" + 'tokio = { workspace = true }') | Set-Content crates/session/Cargo.toml
        @'
        //! Supervisor for a single inherited private pipe connection.
        //!
        //! All exchanges are serialized by mutable ownership. A failed or timed-out
        //! exchange destroys the connection: a possibly committed request is never retried.
        use std::fs::{self, File};
        use std::io;
        use std::path::Path;
        use std::process::Stdio;
        use std::time::Duration;
        
        use lotus_protocol::control::{self, Method, Reply, Request, Status};
        use lotus_protocol::envelope::SessionUuid;
        use tokio::io::{AsyncReadExt, AsyncWriteExt};
        use tokio::process::{Child, ChildStdin, ChildStdout, Command};
        
        use crate::{SessionState, WorkerSpec};
        
        /// Owns the child and its unshared pipe ends. Drop kills the direct child.
        #[derive(Debug)]
        pub struct ControlledWorker {
            child: Child,
            input: ChildStdin,
            output: ChildStdout,
            session: String,
            next_request: u64,
            epoch: u64,
            state: SessionState,
            timeout: Duration,
        }
        
        impl ControlledWorker {
            /// Launch, retain stderr locally, and complete a bounded handshake.
            pub async fn spawn(spec: &WorkerSpec, timeout: Duration) -> io::Result<Self> {
                if timeout.is_zero() || timeout > Duration::from_secs(30) {
                    return Err(io::Error::new(io::ErrorKind::InvalidInput, "timeout must be in (0, 30s]"));
                }
                fs::create_dir_all(&spec.storage_root)?;
                let stderr = File::create(spec.storage_root.join("worker.stderr.log"))?;
                let mut command = Command::new(&spec.executable);
                command.args(&spec.args).envs(spec.env.iter().cloned())
                    .env("LOTUS_STORAGE_ROOT", &spec.storage_root)
                    .stdin(Stdio::piped()).stdout(Stdio::piped()).stderr(stderr)
                    .kill_on_drop(true);
                #[cfg(windows)]
                command.creation_flags(0x0800_0000);
                let mut child = command.spawn()?;
                let input = child.stdin.take().ok_or_else(|| io::Error::other("missing child stdin"))?;
                let output = child.stdout.take().ok_or_else(|| io::Error::other("missing child stdout"))?;
                let mut worker = Self {
                    child, input, output,
                    session: SessionUuid::generate().to_string(),
                    next_request: 1, epoch: 1, state: SessionState::Created, timeout,
                };
                worker.request(Method::Hello).await?;
                worker.state = SessionState::Idle;
                Ok(worker)
            }
        
            /// Current supervisor state; poll status to detect a newly exited process.
            #[must_use]
            pub fn state(&self) -> SessionState { self.state }
        
            /// Child OS identifier, absent after reaping.
            #[must_use]
            pub fn pid(&self) -> Option<u32> { self.child.id() }
        
            /// Query the worker without any GUI dependencies.
            pub async fn status(&mut self) -> io::Result<Reply> { self.request(Method::Status).await }
        
            /// Complete shutdown and reap; kill on any failed exchange or exit deadline.
            pub async fn stop(&mut self) -> io::Result<()> {
                self.request(Method::Stop).await?;
                match tokio::time::timeout(self.timeout, self.child.wait()).await {
                    Ok(Ok(status)) if status.success() => { self.state = SessionState::Stopped; Ok(()) }
                    _ => { self.fail().await; Err(io::Error::other("worker failed to exit cleanly")) }
                }
            }
        
            async fn fail(&mut self) {
                self.state = SessionState::Crashed;
                let _ = self.child.kill().await;
                let _ = self.child.wait().await;
            }
        
            async fn request(&mut self, method: Method) -> io::Result<Reply> {
                if matches!(self.state, SessionState::Stopped | SessionState::Crashed) {
                    return Err(io::Error::new(io::ErrorKind::BrokenPipe, "worker is no longer active"));
                }
                let request = Request {
                    version_major: lotus_protocol::PROTOCOL_VERSION_MAJOR,
                    version_minor: lotus_protocol::PROTOCOL_VERSION_MINOR,
                    request_id: self.next_request, session: self.session.clone(), epoch: self.epoch, method,
                };
                self.next_request = self.next_request.checked_add(1)
                    .ok_or_else(|| io::Error::other("request ID exhausted"))?;
                let result = tokio::time::timeout(self.timeout, self.exchange(&request)).await;
                let reply = match result {
                    Ok(Ok(reply)) => reply,
                    Ok(Err(error)) => { self.fail().await; return Err(error); }
                    Err(_) => {
                        self.fail().await;
                        return Err(io::Error::new(io::ErrorKind::TimedOut, "worker exchange deadline exceeded; result unknown"));
                    }
                };
                if !lotus_protocol::is_compatible(reply.version_major, reply.version_minor)
                    || reply.request_id != request.request_id || reply.session != self.session
                    || reply.epoch != self.epoch || reply.status != Status::Ok
                    || (method == Method::Stop && reply.state != "stopped")
                    || (method != Method::Stop && reply.state != "idle") {
                    self.fail().await;
                    return Err(io::Error::new(io::ErrorKind::InvalidData, "invalid worker reply identity, epoch, status or state"));
                }
                Ok(reply)
            }
        
            async fn exchange(&mut self, request: &Request) -> io::Result<Reply> {
                self.input.write_all(&control::encode(request)?).await?;
                self.input.flush().await?;
                let length = self.output.read_u32_le().await?;
                control::validate_length(length)?;
                let mut payload = vec![0; length as usize];
                self.output.read_exact(&mut payload).await?;
                serde_json::from_slice(&payload).map_err(io::Error::other)
            }
        }

        pub fn mock_path(cli: &Path) -> std::path::PathBuf {
            cli.with_file_name(format!("lotus-mock-worker{}", std::env::consts::EXE_SUFFIX))
        }

        //! Real child-process acceptance, not an in-memory transport simulation.
        use std::time::Duration;
        
        use lotus_session::controlled_worker::ControlledWorker;
        use lotus_session::{SessionState, WorkerSpec};
        
        fn spec(mode: &str) -> WorkerSpec {
            let id = lotus_protocol::envelope::SessionUuid::generate();
            WorkerSpec::new(env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_lotus-mock-worker"),
                std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("lotus-control-{id}"))).arg(mode)
        }
        
        #[tokio::test]
        async fn handshake_query_clean_shutdown_and_second_launch() {
            for _ in 0..2 {
                let spec = spec("");
                let mut worker = ControlledWorker::spawn(&spec, Duration::from_secs(3)).await.expect("mock handshake");
                let reply = worker.status().await.expect("status over pipes");
                assert_eq!(reply.backend, "mock");
                worker.stop().await.expect("graceful exit");
                assert_eq!(worker.state(), SessionState::Stopped);
                assert!(worker.status().await.is_err(), "stopped connection cannot be reused");
                std::fs::remove_dir_all(spec.storage_root).expect("remove test storage");
            }
        }
        
        #[tokio::test]
        async fn failed_handshakes_are_reaped_and_logs_retained() {
            for mode in ["crash", "stale", "hang"] {
                let spec = spec(mode);
                assert!(ControlledWorker::spawn(&spec, Duration::from_millis(500)).await.is_err(), "{mode} must fail");
                assert!(spec.storage_root.join("worker.stderr.log").is_file());
                std::fs::remove_dir_all(spec.storage_root).expect("child has released its files");
            }
        }
        
        #[tokio::test]
        async fn four_private_connections_survive_a_sibling_failure() {
            let mut workers = Vec::new();
            let mut specs = Vec::new();
            for _ in 0..4 {
                let spec = spec("");
                workers.push(ControlledWorker::spawn(&spec, Duration::from_secs(3)).await.expect("spawn isolated child"));
                specs.push(spec);
            }
            assert!(ControlledWorker::spawn(&spec("crash"), Duration::from_secs(3)).await.is_err());
            for (mut worker, spec) in workers.into_iter().zip(specs) {
                worker.status().await.expect("sibling remains responsive");
                worker.stop().await.expect("sibling exits");
                std::fs::remove_dir_all(spec.storage_root).expect("remove test storage");
            }
        }

    impl RenderImage {
        /// Create a new image from the given data.
        pub fn new(data: impl Into<SmallVec<[Frame; 1]>>) -> Self {
            static NEXT_ID: AtomicUsize = AtomicUsize::new(0);
    
            Self {
                id: ImageId(NEXT_ID.fetch_add(1, SeqCst)),
                scale_factor: 1.0,
                data: data.into(),
            }
        }
    
        /// Convert this image into a byte slice.
        pub fn as_bytes(&self, frame_index: usize) -> Option<&[u8]> {
            self.data
                .get(frame_index)
                .map(|frame| frame.buffer().as_raw().as_slice())
        }
    
        /// Get the size of this image, in pixels.
        pub fn size(&self, frame_index: usize) -> Size<DevicePixels> {
            self.data
                .get(frame_index)
                .map(|frame| {
                    let (width, height) = frame.buffer().dimensions();
                    size(width.into(), height.into())
                })
                .unwrap_or_default()
        }
    
        /// Get the size of this image, in pixels for display, adjusted for the scale factor.
        pub(crate) fn render_size(&self, frame_index: usize) -> Size<Pixels> {
            self.size(frame_index)
                .map(|v| (v.0 as f32 / self.scale_factor).into())
        }

    RendererSoftware::RendererSoftware(Core::System& system, Pica::PicaCore& pica_,
                                       Frontend::EmuWindow& window)
        : VideoCore::RendererBase{system, window, nullptr}, memory{system.Memory()}, pica{pica_},
          rasterizer{memory, pica} {}
    
    RendererSoftware::~RendererSoftware() = default;
    
    void RendererSoftware::SwapBuffers() {
        system.perf_stats->StartSwap();
        PrepareRenderTarget();
        system.perf_stats->EndSwap();
        EndFrame();
    }
    
    void RendererSoftware::PrepareRenderTarget() {
        const auto& regs_lcd = pica.regs_lcd;
        for (u32 i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
            const u32 fb_id = i == 2 ? 1 : 0;
    
            const auto color_fill = fb_id == 0 ? regs_lcd.color_fill_top : regs_lcd.color_fill_bottom;
            LoadFBToScreenInfo(i, color_fill);
        }
    }
    
    void RendererSoftware::LoadFBToScreenInfo(int i, const Pica::ColorFill& color_fill) {
        const u32 fb_id = i == 2 ? 1 : 0;
        const auto& framebuffer = pica.regs.framebuffer_config[fb_id];
        auto& info = screen_infos[i];
    
        const PAddr framebuffer_addr =
            framebuffer.active_fb == 0 ? framebuffer.address_left1 : framebuffer.address_left2;
        const s32 bpp = Pica::BytesPerPixel(framebuffer.color_format);
        const u8* framebuffer_data = memory.GetPhysicalPointer(framebuffer_addr);
    
        const s32 pixel_stride = framebuffer.stride / bpp;
        info.height = framebuffer.height;
        info.width = pixel_stride;
        info.pixels.resize(info.width * info.height * 4);
    
        for (u32 y = 0; y < info.height; y++) {
            for (u32 x = 0; x < info.width; x++) {
                const u8* pixel = framebuffer_data + (y * pixel_stride + pixel_stride - x) * bpp;
                Common::Vec4 color = [&] {
                    if (color_fill.is_enabled) {
                        return Common::Vec4<u8>(color_fill.color_r, color_fill.color_g,
                                                color_fill.color_b, 255);
                    }
    
                    switch (framebuffer.color_format) {
                    case Pica::PixelFormat::RGBA8:
                        return Common::Color::DecodeRGBA8(pixel);
                    case Pica::PixelFormat::RGB8:
                        return Common::Color::DecodeRGB8(pixel);
                    case Pica::PixelFormat::RGB565:
                        return Common::Color::DecodeRGB565(pixel);
                    case Pica::PixelFormat::RGB5A1:
                        return Common::Color::DecodeRGB5A1(pixel);
                    case Pica::PixelFormat::RGBA4:
                        return Common::Color::DecodeRGBA4(pixel);
                    }
                    UNREACHABLE();
                }();
                const u32 output_offset = (x * info.height + y) * 4;
                u8* dest = info.pixels.data() + output_offset;
                std::memcpy(dest, color.AsArray(), sizeof(color));
            }
        }
    }

     * For smooth Vsync rendering, we want to always present the latest frame that the core generates,
     * but also make sure that rendering happens at the pace that the frontend dictates. This is a
     * helper class that the renderer can define to sync frames between the render thread and the
     * presentation thread
     */
    class TextureMailbox {
    public:
        virtual ~TextureMailbox() = default;
    
        /**
         * Recreate the render objects attached to this frame with the new specified width/height
         */
        virtual void ReloadRenderFrame(Frontend::Frame* frame, u32 width, u32 height) = 0;
    
        /**
         * Recreate the presentation objects attached to this frame with the new specified width/height
         */
        virtual void ReloadPresentFrame(Frontend::Frame* frame, u32 width, u32 height) = 0;
    
        /**
         * Render thread calls this to get an available frame to present
         */
        virtual Frontend::Frame* GetRenderFrame() = 0;
    
        /**
         * Render thread calls this after draw commands are done to add to the presentation mailbox
         */
        virtual void ReleaseRenderFrame(Frame* frame) = 0;
    
        /**
         * Presentation thread calls this to get the latest frame available to present. If there is no
         * frame available after timeout, returns the previous frame. If there is no previous frame it
         * returns nullptr
         */
        virtual Frontend::Frame* TryGetPresentFrame(int timeout_ms) = 0;
    };

        class Scoped {
        public:
            explicit Scoped(GraphicsContext& context_) : context(context_) {
                context.MakeCurrent();
            }
            ~Scoped() {
                context.DoneCurrent();
            }
    
        private:
            GraphicsContext& context;
        };
    
        /// Calls MakeCurrent on the context and calls DoneCurrent when the scope for the returned value
        /// ends
        [[nodiscard]] Scoped Acquire() {
            return Scoped{*this};
        }

            std::fs::remove_dir_all(spec.storage_root).expect("reaped child releases log");

        # T03: inherited private control pipes
        
        Status: **verified compiled** on Windows GNU; process acceptance tests executed.
        No Azahar emulation is advertised by this spike. Source baseline:
        `11eceda5e0e682a1f44e396bf954a1b9137097ca`; no native files changed.
        
        ## Decision
        
        The supervisor creates the worker with inherited stdin/stdout pipe ends. There
        is no socket name to guess, public listener, or reconnect operation. Possession
        of the inherited handles is the capability. This implements the local-pipe
        option without introducing a discoverable named-pipe server. A later attach
        feature must add explicit OS access control and secure authentication.
        
        Each message is a four-byte little-endian unsigned byte count followed by UTF-8
        JSON. The count must be in 1..=65536 before allocation. Schema:
        `specs/control-v1.schema.json`; executable types: `protocol::control`.
        The existing fixed C ABI structs are unchanged. The larger protocol draft is
        still proposed; no native worker compatibility is claimed.
        
        The connection starts with hello, session identity and epoch 1; status and stop
        follow. Replies echo identity, request number and epoch. Unknown fields/methods,
        incompatible versions, malformed/truncated/oversized frames and unexpected
        reply identities are rejected. A mutable client owns the single outstanding
        exchange. Deadlines cover writes as well as reads. On transport failure or
        ambiguous timeout the child is killed/reaped; mutations are never retried.
        Stderr remains under the supplied private root. Clean stop requires both the
        completion reply and successful child exit.
        
        ## Reproduction
        
        ```powershell
        cargo test -p lotus-protocol -p lotus-session -p lotus-cli
        cargo build -p lotus-cli -p lotus-session
        .\target\debug\ctr-cli.exe mock .\target\debug\lotus-mock-worker.exe
        ```
        
        Tests cover clean exit and second launch, four simultaneous children, sibling
        failure, handshake crash/hang/stale epoch, crash after handshake and framing
        limits. The concurrent test exposed duplicate time-derived session UUIDs on
        Windows; an atomic counter now guarantees uniqueness within the process.
        Identifiers are not authentication secrets.
        
        ## Limits and rollback
        
        Linux/macOS are untested. This is T03 process infrastructure, not T09: drop
        kills the direct child; descendant job containment, storage locks, native
        capabilities and emulation commands remain to be implemented. The old scaffold
        WorkerProcess remains untouched. No guest output/performance claim applies;
        only host process/control behavior is exercised. Remove the CLI mock command
        and new modules to roll back without changing native behavior.
